name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: In performing audit procedures, auditors commonly use data from which two primary sources?

answers.text: Entity-produced data (accounting records, transaction files, master files) and external data (market prices, third-party records, industry benchmarks)
Data from the prior-year audit workpapers only — current-year data is prepared exclusively by management
Data from regulatory agencies and government databases exclusively — entity-produced data is not reliable for audit purposes
Oral representations from management and verbal confirmations from customers — documentary data is not required

explanations.a: AU-C Section 500 recognizes that audit evidence comes from two broad sources: (1) entity-produced data — including accounting records (general ledger, subsidiary ledgers), transaction files (purchase orders, invoices, receiving reports), master files (customer files, vendor files), and entity-prepared reports (aged receivables listings, inventory compilations); and (2) external data — including market prices from external data providers, industry benchmarks, confirmation responses from third parties, and regulatory filings. The auditor uses both types, evaluating the reliability of each based on its source and how it was obtained.
explanations.b: Current-year entity-produced data is a primary source of audit evidence — it is not limited to prior-year workpapers. Prior-year workpapers provide context and planning information, but current-year testing relies on current-period data from the entity and external sources.
explanations.c: While external sources are generally more reliable than entity-produced data, auditors extensively use entity-produced data. The reliability of entity data depends on the effectiveness of controls over its preparation — it is not inherently unusable for audit purposes.
explanations.d: Oral representations and verbal confirmations are generally lower-reliability evidence. Documentary evidence — written records, electronic data files, and written confirmations — is the primary form of audit evidence. Oral representations are supplemental but not the primary evidentiary base.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: Before using an entity-provided transaction data file to perform audit sampling, an auditor should verify the completeness and accuracy of the file. Which procedure is MOST appropriate for this purpose?

answers.text: Ask management to sign a written representation confirming that the data file is complete and accurate
Randomly select 10 items from the file and verify them manually to the accounting records
Reconcile the file's record counts and total dollar amounts to independently prepared control totals — such as summary reports from the entity's accounting system or the trial balance
Accept the data file without testing since management prepared it using the same system used to prepare the financial statements

explanations.a: Management's representation confirms that the file is complete and accurate per management's belief — but it does not independently verify the data. The representation is not corroborated evidence of data integrity; independent reconciliation is a more reliable verification procedure.
explanations.b: Verifying 10 randomly selected items confirms the accuracy of those specific items but does not verify the completeness of the file — it would not detect records that are missing from the file entirely. Completeness testing requires comparison at the total population level, not just individual item testing.
explanations.c: Reconciling record counts (total number of transactions in the file) and total dollar amounts to independent control totals — such as totals from the entity's accounting system summary reports, the trial balance, or bank statements — provides evidence that the file contains all records (completeness) and that the amounts are accurate (accuracy). If the file reconciles to these independently prepared totals, the auditor has reasonable assurance that the data is complete and accurate for audit use.
explanations.d: A data file extracted from the accounting system may not be complete — extraction errors, filter errors, or incomplete date ranges can cause missing records. The fact that the same system was used to prepare the financial statements does not guarantee that the extraction was complete and accurate.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: An auditor downloads a revenue transaction file and applies several data transformations — filtering by date range, excluding intercompany transactions, and aggregating by customer — before performing an analytical procedure. The primary reason the auditor must document these transformations in the workpapers is

answers.text: To satisfy a regulatory disclosure requirement that data transformations be reported to the SEC

To ensure that the analysis can be reproduced, reviewed, and understood by any experienced auditor reviewing the workpapers — and to demonstrate that transformations did not inadvertently exclude or misclassify transactions relevant to the procedure
To provide evidence of the auditor's technical proficiency in data manipulation for quality control purposes
Documentation is not required for data transformations since they are a preparatory step rather than an audit procedure

explanations.a: No SEC disclosure requirement applies to the documentation of auditor data transformations. Documentation requirements are professional standards-based (AU-C 230 — Audit Documentation), not SEC regulatory requirements.
explanations.b: AU-C Section 230 requires the auditor to document audit procedures performed in sufficient detail to enable an experienced auditor with no prior connection to the engagement to understand the nature, timing, and extent of procedures. When data transformations are applied, documenting them serves to: (1) demonstrate that the analysis is reproducible and the conclusions are based on a specific, defined dataset; (2) show that the transformations were appropriate (the date filter captured the right period, the intercompany exclusion was correct, the aggregation logic was sound); and (3) reveal if any transformations inadvertently excluded records that should have been included or included records that should have been excluded — which would affect the validity of the analytical result.
explanations.c: While documenting procedures reflects professional competence, the primary purpose of workpaper documentation is to enable independent review and reproduction of the audit work — not to demonstrate the auditor's technical skills.
explanations.d: Data transformations are integral steps in the analytical procedure, not merely preparatory steps exempt from documentation. The transformation decisions (what to filter, how to aggregate) directly affect the result of the analysis and must be documented as part of the procedure.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: An auditor requests a complete accounts payable transaction file from the entity to use as the population for sampling. Upon reconciling the file to the trial balance, the auditor finds the file total is $2.3 million less than the accounts payable balance on the trial balance — a 3.1% difference. Management provides a general explanation that 'some year-end accruals may not have been captured in the extract.' The auditor intends to proceed with sampling using the file. Which assessment is MOST appropriate?

answers.text: Proceeding is appropriate since 3.1% is below the auditor's materiality threshold and management has provided an explanation
Proceeding is appropriate if the auditor reduces the sampling risk allowance by 3.1% to compensate for the missing population
Proceeding is appropriate since management's explanation is plausible and the file represents 96.9% of the population

Proceeding without resolving the $2.3 million discrepancy is inappropriate — the unreconciled population means the sampling results cannot be validly extrapolated to the full accounts payable balance; the auditor must investigate the discrepancy and either obtain a complete file or modify the audit approach

explanations.a: Materiality thresholds apply to misstatements in the financial statements — they do not set the threshold for accepting data file discrepancies before using the file as a sampling population. A 3.1% discrepancy in the population file means the sampling results represent only 96.9% of the balance, not the total. The unexplained gap represents potential uncovered audit risk.
explanations.b: Arbitrarily reducing the sampling risk allowance by the discrepancy percentage is not a valid statistical or professional response to an unreconciled population. Sampling risk quantification assumes the sample is drawn from the complete population — a materially incomplete population invalidates statistical extrapolation.
explanations.c: Management's explanation is vague ('some year-end accruals may not have been captured') and is not corroborated. The auditor cannot evaluate whether the $2.3 million represents a systematic omission of certain types of accruals, whether it is itself evidence of an understatement, or whether the explanation is accurate without further investigation.
explanations.d: Audit sampling produces conclusions that are extrapolated from the sample to the entire defined population. If the population used for sampling (the file) is known to be incomplete by $2.3 million, the auditor's projected findings cannot be reliably extrapolated to the full accounts payable balance — the sampling results will systematically miss the unrepresented portion. The auditor must: obtain a complete file that reconciles to the trial balance; understand and verify the nature of the discrepancy (are the missing accruals legitimate year-end entries?); and either use a complete population or modify the approach to address the unrepresented items separately.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: Which of the following general principles BEST describes the relative reliability of audit evidence?

answers.text: Oral representations from management are more reliable than documentary evidence because they reflect current management knowledge
Photocopies of documents are always as reliable as originals since modern copying technology produces exact reproductions

Evidence obtained directly by the auditor (e.g., through observation or physical inspection) and evidence from external independent sources are generally more reliable than entity-produced evidence obtained from management
All types of audit evidence are equally reliable — the auditor must assess sufficiency only, not quality

explanations.a: Oral representations from management are the least reliable form of audit evidence because they are not independently verifiable and are subject to management bias. Documentary evidence — particularly from external sources — is significantly more reliable.
explanations.b: Photocopies and electronic reproductions are generally less reliable than originals because they can be falsified without obvious detection. The auditor should evaluate whether circumstances suggest that copies may not faithfully reproduce the original documents.
explanations.c: AU-C Section 500 provides a reliability hierarchy: evidence obtained directly by the auditor (through inspection, observation, or computation) is generally more reliable than evidence provided by the entity; and evidence from independent external sources (bank confirmations, attorney letters, independent appraisals) is generally more reliable than internally generated entity evidence. These principles guide the auditor in designing procedures that provide the most persuasive evidence available.
explanations.d: Not all audit evidence is equally reliable — quality (appropriateness) is a fundamental dimension of evidence evaluation alongside quantity (sufficiency). More reliable evidence can reduce the quantity needed to reach a conclusion.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: An auditor is evaluating the reliability of an internally generated accounts receivable aging report that will be used to test the adequacy of the allowance for doubtful accounts. Which factor MOST affects the reliability of this report?

answers.text: The effectiveness of the entity's controls over the preparation of accounting reports — including access controls, review procedures, and reconciliation of the aging report to the accounts receivable subsidiary ledger
The age of the entity — older companies produce more reliable data because they have longer operating histories
The number of customers on the aging report — reports with more customers are inherently more reliable because they represent a larger dataset
Whether the report was prepared on a Saturday or a weekday — timing of preparation affects data reliability

explanations.a: AU-C Section 500 specifically notes that the reliability of internally generated information as audit evidence is affected by the effectiveness of the entity's controls over the preparation of that information. For an accounts receivable aging report, the relevant controls include: access controls (preventing unauthorized modification of the underlying receivables data); review procedures (supervisory review comparing the aging to prior periods and to supporting data); and reconciliation procedures (ensuring the aging report totals agree to the accounts receivable subsidiary ledger and general ledger). Strong controls over these processes increase the reliability of the aging report as audit evidence.
explanations.b: The entity's age has no systematic relationship to the reliability of its data. A young company with strong automated controls and IT infrastructure may produce more reliable data than an older company with legacy systems and weak controls.
explanations.c: The number of records in a report affects the coverage of the evidence (how many customers are represented) — but it does not directly affect the reliability of the data. A large aging report with weak controls is less reliable than a smaller report with strong controls.
explanations.d: The day of week a report is prepared has no bearing on its reliability. Reliability depends on the quality of the underlying data and the controls over its preparation — not the timing of the extraction.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: During testing, an auditor inspects vendor invoices and discovers that several original invoices appear to have been replaced with photocopies. The auditor's MOST appropriate response is to

answers.text: Accept the photocopies as equivalent to originals since the amounts and vendor names appear consistent with other records
Exclude the photocopied invoices from the test sample and use only original documents, resulting in a smaller effective sample size

Document the observation and consider whether additional procedures are needed to corroborate the amounts represented by the photocopied invoices — for example, by obtaining confirmation from vendors or examining additional supporting documentation
Discard the findings from all invoices and start the entire test over using a fresh sample

explanations.a: Accepting photocopies that replaced originals at face value, without investigation, ignores the risk that the substitution occurred to conceal alterations. AU-C 500 notes that photocopies are generally less reliable than originals — when photocopies appear to have replaced originals without explanation, the auditor must investigate.
explanations.b: Excluding the photocopied invoices and reducing the sample size would leave the auditor with insufficient evidence for the sampled population items represented by those invoices, and would not address the potential misstatement or fraud indicated by the substitution.
explanations.c: When original documents appear to have been replaced by photocopies, the auditor should: document the finding in the workpapers; investigate the reason for the substitution (were the originals lost or intentionally replaced?); apply professional skepticism — the substitution may indicate an attempt to alter or fabricate documentation; and perform additional corroborating procedures for the affected items, such as obtaining direct confirmation from the vendor of the amounts and transaction details, or examining alternative supporting documents (purchase orders, receiving reports, contract terms).
explanations.d: Discarding all findings and restarting the test would lose the information already gathered (including the observation about the photocopies, which is itself significant) and would be inefficient. The appropriate response is targeted investigation of the specific anomaly, not wholesale repetition.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: An auditor confirms an accounts receivable balance directly with the customer and receives a written confirmation indicating the amount is $450,000. The entity's accounting records show $620,000 for the same customer account. Management explains the $170,000 difference as items shipped to the customer in December that were not yet received by the customer at confirmation date. How should the auditor evaluate this conflicting evidence?

answers.text: Accept management's explanation without further testing since in-transit shipments are a common and reasonable explanation for confirmation differences
Discard the confirmation response since a difference was found and the confirmation is therefore unreliable

Investigate the $170,000 difference by examining shipping records (bills of lading, freight invoices, delivery confirmations) to determine whether the December shipments actually occurred and whether revenue was appropriately recognized at the shipping date
Treat the entire $620,000 balance as uncollectible since the customer only acknowledges $450,000

explanations.a: Accepting management's explanation without corroboration is insufficient when a material difference exists between an independently confirmed amount and the recorded balance. In-transit shipments are a plausible explanation, but plausibility is not the same as verified truth. The explanation must be corroborated by objective evidence.
explanations.b: A confirmation difference is not a reason to discard the confirmation response — it is important audit evidence that must be investigated. The difference itself is informative and requires resolution, not dismissal of the entire confirmation.
explanations.c: When a customer's confirmation response differs from the recorded balance, the auditor must investigate the difference. For a difference attributed to in-transit shipments, the appropriate corroborating procedures include: inspecting the shipping documentation for the claimed December shipments (bills of lading with shipping dates, freight invoices, carrier tracking information); verifying that the shipment terms (FOB shipping point vs. FOB destination) support recognition at the shipping date; and confirming with the customer whether goods were received after the confirmation date. These procedures either corroborate or contradict management's explanation.
explanations.d: A difference between the confirmed balance and the recorded balance does not mean the entire balance is uncollectible — the difference may reflect timing (in-transit items not yet received by the customer) rather than a collection risk. Treating the full balance as uncollectible would be an overreaction not supported by the evidence at hand.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: Data analytics in auditing enables auditors to

answers.text: Replace professional judgment entirely — data analytics algorithms automatically determine which financial statement assertions are fairly stated
Analyze large populations of transactions to identify patterns, anomalies, outliers, or trends that may indicate areas of higher risk of misstatement
Eliminate the need for any other form of audit evidence since analytics covers all transactions
Access the entity's computer systems without management's knowledge or consent

explanations.a: Data analytics is a tool that assists auditors — it does not replace professional judgment. The auditor must still design the analytics, evaluate their results, determine which anomalies or patterns warrant follow-up, and form conclusions based on the full body of evidence. Algorithms do not make audit judgments.
explanations.b: A key benefit of data analytics is the ability to efficiently process and analyze large datasets — potentially entire populations of transactions rather than samples. This allows auditors to identify patterns (recurring transactions with specific characteristics), anomalies (transactions that deviate from expected patterns), outliers (amounts significantly different from the rest of the population), and trends (changes in transaction volumes or amounts over time) that may indicate heightened risk of material misstatement.
explanations.c: Data analytics enhances and extends the reach of audit testing but does not replace all other forms of evidence. Results from analytics testing typically lead to additional follow-up procedures (examining specific anomalous transactions, obtaining documentation) rather than standing alone as complete audit evidence.
explanations.d: Auditors access entity systems through proper authorization from management as part of the planned audit procedures — not covertly or without consent. Access to entity data requires appropriate engagement-level authorization.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: An auditor applies Benford's Law to the entity's accounts payable disbursement file. Benford's Law analysis in an audit is used to

answers.text: Calculate the mathematical probability that any specific invoice is fraudulent
Replace tests of controls for the accounts payable function
Eliminate the need for accounts payable confirmations from vendors

Identify transactions with digit patterns that deviate significantly from naturally expected distributions — deviations may indicate data manipulation, fabricated amounts, or anomalies warranting further investigation

explanations.a: Benford's Law analysis identifies statistical anomalies in digit patterns — it does not calculate the probability that specific transactions are fraudulent. Anomalies are indicators that warrant investigation, not proof of fraud.
explanations.b: Benford's Law analysis is a substantive analytical procedure — it tests the characteristics of the transaction data population. It does not test the operating effectiveness of controls (which is the purpose of tests of controls). The two procedures address different assertions and risk dimensions.
explanations.c: Vendor confirmation procedures provide independent third-party verification of account balances. Benford's Law analysis examines the internal pattern of digits in recorded amounts — it addresses a different risk and cannot substitute for the independent corroboration that confirmations provide.
explanations.d: Benford's Law states that in naturally occurring datasets (such as financial transaction amounts), the leading digit is '1' approximately 30% of the time, '2' about 18%, and so on in a decreasing logarithmic distribution. Fabricated amounts often do not follow this distribution — people tend to make up numbers starting with digits 5, 6, 7, or 8, or use round numbers. Applying Benford's Law to disbursements or other transaction data identifies digit patterns that deviate from expected natural distributions — which may indicate data manipulation, fabricated invoices, or amounts that were selected non-randomly (e.g., amounts just below approval thresholds).

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: An auditor uses data analytics to test the complete population of journal entries for the year, searching for entries with characteristics associated with fraud risk — entries posted by users without accounting authority, entries with round-dollar amounts, and entries posted outside normal business hours. How does this approach DIFFER from traditional sample-based journal entry testing?

answers.text: Population-based analytics reduces audit quality because it cannot evaluate the business purpose of individual entries as effectively as detailed sample testing
Population-based analytics requires the auditor to obtain management approval for each entry reviewed, which is more time-consuming than sample selection
There is no difference — data analytics and sample-based testing produce identical results for journal entry populations

Population-based analytics identifies every entry exhibiting the specified risk characteristics across the entire population — allowing the auditor to focus investigation on the highest-risk entries; sample-based testing covers only a subset of entries and may miss high-risk entries not selected in the sample

explanations.a: Population-based analytics significantly improves the detection capability for entries with specific risk characteristics — it identifies all entries meeting the defined criteria, not just those that happened to be selected in a sample. This does not reduce audit quality — it enhances it. Evaluating the business purpose of specific high-risk entries identified by analytics is a follow-up procedure that the auditor performs after the analytics identify the flagged items.
explanations.b: Analytics results are evaluated by the auditor using professional judgment — management approval is not required for each entry reviewed. The auditor independently evaluates the entries flagged by the analytics without management pre-approval.
explanations.c: The difference is fundamental: sample-based testing provides a statistical estimate based on a subset; population-based analytics identifies every entry meeting the specified criteria. The two approaches produce different types of conclusions and different coverage.
explanations.d: This accurately distinguishes the two approaches. Traditional journal entry sampling — even with targeted selection criteria — covers a fraction of the total population and relies on probabilistic inference to reach conclusions about the full set of entries. If a fraudulent journal entry is not selected in the sample, it will not be detected. Population-based data analytics applies the search criteria to every entry in the dataset, ensuring that no entry meeting the fraud-risk criteria is overlooked — the auditor then investigates the flagged items to determine whether they represent actual misstatements.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: An auditor applies multiple data analytics techniques to the revenue transaction population and finds no anomalies — all transactions fall within expected patterns on every test applied. The auditor concludes that no material misstatements exist in revenue. Is this conclusion appropriate?

answers.text: Yes — population-based analytics covering all transactions eliminates the need for additional substantive procedures in revenue
Yes — when all analytics tests produce expected results, the auditor has obtained sufficient evidence to support an unmodified opinion without further revenue testing

No — data analytics tests are designed to detect specific patterns or anomalies; misstatements may exist in forms that are not captured by the particular analytics applied, and professional judgment is required to determine what additional procedures are needed
No — data analytics results are never reliable enough to inform audit conclusions; traditional sample testing must always be used instead

explanations.a: Population-based analytics does not eliminate the need for additional substantive procedures. Analytics identify patterns and anomalies within defined parameters — they test what they are designed to test and no more. A clean analytics result means no items were flagged by the specific criteria applied, not that no misstatements exist.
explanations.b: Reaching an unmodified opinion based solely on analytics results — without other substantive procedures — would not constitute sufficient appropriate audit evidence. Analytics results require professional judgment and typically lead to targeted follow-up testing rather than standing alone as complete evidence for a significant account.
explanations.c: Each data analytics test is designed around specific patterns or anomalies (e.g., Benford's Law tests digit patterns; an outlier analysis identifies unusual amounts). If revenue misstatements exist in a form the auditor did not specifically test for — for example, fictitious transactions recorded at amounts consistent with real transactions, or missing transactions (completeness issues not addressed by the tests used) — the analytics would not flag them. The auditor must evaluate what forms of misstatement the applied analytics are capable of detecting and design additional procedures to address risks not covered by the analytics.
explanations.d: Data analytics results are valuable audit evidence — this option overstates their limitations. The issue is not that analytics are unreliable; it is that their conclusions are limited to the specific patterns they were designed to detect, not the full range of potential misstatements.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: The concept of 'sufficient appropriate audit evidence' requires that evidence be both sufficient and appropriate. What do these two qualities mean?

answers.text: Sufficient means the evidence was gathered in a timely manner; appropriate means the evidence is from an external source
Sufficient means all transactions have been tested 100%; appropriate means each transaction has at least two pieces of supporting documentation
Sufficient means the evidence was obtained at year-end rather than at an interim date; appropriate means the evidence addresses all five financial statement assertions simultaneously

Sufficient relates to the quantity of evidence — how much is needed to support the auditor's conclusions; appropriate relates to the quality of evidence — its relevance to the specific assertion tested and its reliability as a basis for that conclusion

explanations.a: Timeliness of evidence gathering is not what 'sufficient' means — sufficiency is about quantity. The source of evidence (external vs. internal) is a factor in reliability, which contributes to appropriateness — but appropriateness also encompasses relevance, not just source.
explanations.b: 100% transaction testing would be more than sufficient for most purposes, but sufficiency does not require testing everything. Sufficient evidence means enough evidence to support the conclusion — not necessarily complete population coverage. The '2 documents per transaction' criterion is not how appropriateness is defined.
explanations.c: Timing (year-end vs. interim) is a factor the auditor considers in designing procedures, but it is not the definition of sufficiency. Appropriateness encompasses relevance and reliability — not whether evidence addresses all assertions simultaneously.
explanations.d: AU-C Section 500 defines these concepts clearly: sufficiency is the measure of the quantity of audit evidence — more evidence is needed when the risk of material misstatement is higher or when individual pieces of evidence are less reliable. Appropriateness is the measure of quality — comprising two dimensions: (1) relevance — whether the evidence pertains to the specific assertion being tested (an inventory count observation provides relevant evidence for the existence assertion, but less so for the valuation assertion); and (2) reliability — how credible and trustworthy the evidence is as a basis for the conclusion (directly obtained evidence is more reliable than entity-provided evidence).

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: When the auditor assesses a HIGH risk of material misstatement for the valuation assertion in investments, how does this assessment affect the quantity and quality of evidence required?

answers.text: High RMM reduces the evidence requirement since the auditor's attention is already focused on this area
High RMM requires either more evidence (larger samples, more procedures) or evidence of higher quality (from more reliable sources) — or both — to bring audit risk to an acceptably low level
High RMM only affects the timing of procedures — all evidence must be gathered at year-end rather than at an interim date
High RMM has no effect on evidence requirements since the auditor's overall materiality threshold covers all risk levels equally

explanations.a: High RMM increases — not reduces — the evidence requirement. The inverse relationship between RMM and evidence: when the risk of misstatement is high, more or better evidence is needed to reach the same level of assurance about the assertion.
explanations.b: The audit risk model (Audit Risk = RMM × Detection Risk) requires that when RMM is high, detection risk must be reduced to bring overall audit risk to an acceptably low level. Detection risk is reduced by: increasing the quantity of evidence gathered (larger samples, more procedures covering the assertion); obtaining evidence from more reliable sources (independent confirmations rather than management-provided schedules, specialist opinions rather than management estimates); or both. A high-risk assertion cannot be adequately addressed with the same quantity and quality of evidence used for a lower-risk assertion.
explanations.c: Timing is one of the three dimensions of audit response (nature, timing, extent) — but it is not the only factor affected by high RMM. High RMM affects all three dimensions. Additionally, high RMM does not automatically require year-end rather than interim testing — the auditor must assess whether interim testing can be effectively updated.
explanations.d: Materiality is about the size of misstatements that would matter to users — it is not a risk-covering mechanism that makes evidence requirements uniform across all risk levels. Evidence requirements are driven by RMM, not by materiality alone.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: An auditor relies heavily on management's written representations as evidence for the fair value of a significant investment portfolio. This is MOST problematic because

answers.text: Management representations are not a recognized form of audit evidence under GAAS
Written representations are required to be in the client's handwriting to be valid audit evidence

Management representations are inherently limited in reliability for fair value measurements — they represent management's own assertions and lack the independence and corroboration of external or directly obtained evidence; relying primarily on them for a significant, judgment-intensive valuation does not constitute sufficient appropriate audit evidence
Representations from management are only appropriate for qualitative disclosures, not for quantitative balance sheet amounts

explanations.a: Management representations are a recognized form of audit evidence under AU-C Section 580 — the auditor is required to obtain them for certain matters. The issue is not whether they are recognized evidence but whether relying on them as the primary evidence for a complex fair value measurement provides sufficient appropriate evidence.
explanations.b: There is no requirement that representations be in the client's handwriting. Written representations are typically prepared as a formal letter signed by management (CEO and CFO typically) — the handwriting format requirement does not exist.
explanations.c: AU-C Section 500 acknowledges that evidence from independent sources is more reliable than evidence from the entity itself. Management representations about fair value are management's self-assessments — they do not independently corroborate the value. For a significant investment portfolio with complex valuations, the auditor needs evidence such as: prices from independent pricing services; appraisals from an auditor's specialist; comparison to observable market transactions; or independent recalculation of valuations. AU-C 580 explicitly states that written representations do not provide sufficient appropriate audit evidence on their own — they supplement, not replace, other evidence.
explanations.d: Management representations are used for various matters including quantitative balance sheet amounts (e.g., representations about completeness of disclosed liabilities, absence of undisclosed related-party transactions). The limitation is about their reliability for specific high-risk areas, not a categorical restriction to qualitative matters.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: An auditor cannot obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence for the revenue recognition assertion because management has denied access to certain customer contracts that it claims contain proprietary terms. The auditor cannot obtain the needed evidence through alternative procedures. Which response is MOST appropriate?

answers.text: Expand testing of other revenue-related accounts (accounts receivable, deferred revenue) to compensate for the missing contract evidence
Accept management's representation that the contracts support the recorded revenue and issue an unmodified opinion

Communicate the limitation to management and those charged with governance, and consider whether the inability to obtain sufficient evidence requires a qualified opinion (if the limitation is material but not pervasive) or a disclaimer of opinion (if the limitation is pervasive)
Issue an adverse opinion since management-imposed scope limitations always result in adverse opinions

explanations.a: Testing other revenue-related accounts (receivables, deferred revenue) provides corroborating evidence about some revenue assertions, but it does not substitute for evidence specifically addressing the revenue recognition assertion for the contracts at issue. If the contracts define the performance obligations, transaction price, and satisfaction conditions, the inability to review them leaves a gap in evidence that cannot be fully compensated by testing related balance sheet accounts.
explanations.b: Management's representation about contract terms is not sufficient appropriate evidence for the revenue recognition assertion — particularly when the contracts themselves have been denied to the auditor. Relying on management's assertion about content management has deliberately withheld significantly undermines the quality of the evidence.
explanations.c: A management-imposed scope limitation that prevents the auditor from obtaining sufficient appropriate evidence for a material assertion requires the auditor to: (1) communicate the limitation to management and TCWG; (2) evaluate whether alternative procedures can provide the needed evidence (if not available, the limitation remains); and (3) consider the appropriate opinion modification. AU-C Section 705 specifies: if the limitation is material but not pervasive (affects only a specific area), a qualified opinion ('except for' the effects of the limitation) is appropriate; if the limitation is so fundamental and pervasive that the auditor cannot form any opinion on the financial statements, a disclaimer of opinion is required.
explanations.d: A management-imposed scope limitation does not automatically result in an adverse opinion. An adverse opinion is issued when the financial statements are materially and pervasively misstated — not when evidence is unavailable. The appropriate response to a scope limitation is a qualified opinion or disclaimer of opinion, not an adverse opinion.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: For a given audit, an auditor obtains two pieces of evidence relating to the existence assertion for accounts receivable: (1) an aging report prepared by management reconciling to the trial balance; and (2) positive confirmation responses from customers representing 72% of the total balance. Which statement BEST describes how these two pieces of evidence should be evaluated together?

answers.text: Since two pieces of evidence exist, sufficient appropriate evidence has been obtained regardless of their quality or what they cover
The management-prepared aging report should be disregarded entirely since it comes from an internal source and lacks independence

Both pieces of evidence are relevant but have different reliability levels — the customer confirmations are more reliable (independent, external) but cover only 72% of the balance; the aging report is lower reliability but covers 100%; together they inform the overall assessment, but the auditor must still address the unconfirmed 28% through alternative procedures
The auditor should average the reliability of the two pieces of evidence to arrive at a blended reliability score for the overall conclusion

explanations.a: The number of evidence pieces is not the determining factor in sufficiency — it is the overall persuasiveness of the evidence relative to the risk. Two pieces of low-quality evidence that cover the same aspect of an assertion may be less useful than one piece of high-quality evidence from an independent source.
explanations.b: Internally generated evidence is not inherently useless — its reliability depends on the effectiveness of controls over its preparation. An aging report reconciled to the trial balance with effective IT and review controls provides meaningful corroborating evidence, even though it is less reliable than independent confirmations.
explanations.c: This accurately describes how the auditor should use the two evidence types together. Customer confirmations are the most reliable evidence for the existence and accuracy assertions of accounts receivable — they represent independent, external, directly obtained corroboration from the parties who owe the amounts. The aging report provides broader coverage and corroborating context, but with lower inherent reliability. The combination provides coverage of most of the balance, but the auditor must perform alternative procedures (examining subsequent cash receipts, reviewing shipping documents, or applying analytical procedures) on the unconfirmed 28% to address the existence and collectability assertions for those items.
explanations.d: Evidence quality is not evaluated by mathematical averaging. Different pieces of evidence address different aspects of assertions with different degrees of reliability — they are combined through professional judgment, not a blended score formula.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: Audit sampling is defined as applying an audit procedure to

answers.text: Less than 100% of items within a population relevant to the audit, where each sampling unit has a chance of selection, to provide a reasonable basis for conclusions about the entire population
100% of items within a population to provide absolute assurance about the population
Items selected entirely at the auditor's discretion from the largest-dollar transactions in a population
A fixed number of items (typically 25) from any size population, regardless of the risk of material misstatement

explanations.a: AU-C Section 530 defines audit sampling as applying audit procedures to less than 100% of items within a relevant population, where each sampling unit has a chance of selection, to enable the auditor to reach conclusions about the entire population. The three essential elements are: (1) less than 100% coverage (otherwise it is complete population testing, not sampling); (2) each unit has a chance of selection (random or systematic selection is required for statistical sampling; judgmental selection is used in nonstatistical sampling); and (3) the purpose is to support conclusions about the full population.
explanations.b: Testing 100% of items is complete population testing — not sampling. Audit sampling specifically refers to procedures applied to less than the full population.
explanations.c: Selecting only the largest-dollar items is a targeted selection approach — sometimes called specific item selection or directed testing. While legitimate in certain circumstances, it is not sampling because items below the threshold have no chance of selection, preventing the auditor from reaching statistical conclusions about the entire population.
explanations.d: A fixed sample size of 25 regardless of population size or risk is not aligned with professional standards. Sample size must be responsive to assessed risk, the population size, tolerable misstatement, and expected error rate — not a fixed predetermined number.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: Which of the following BEST distinguishes statistical sampling from nonstatistical sampling in an audit?

answers.text: Statistical sampling always produces larger samples than nonstatistical sampling since it is based on mathematical formulas
Nonstatistical sampling requires more extensive documentation than statistical sampling since it relies on professional judgment

Statistical sampling uses random or systematic selection and allows the auditor to mathematically quantify and control sampling risk — nonstatistical sampling relies on professional judgment throughout and cannot quantify sampling risk
Statistical sampling is only available for tests of controls, while nonstatistical sampling is used for tests of details

explanations.a: Statistical sampling does not always produce larger samples. Sample sizes in statistical sampling are determined mathematically based on risk, precision, and expected error rates — and may in some cases be smaller than nonstatistical samples selected by an auditor applying conservative judgment.
explanations.b: Professional standards require documentation of sampling procedures for both statistical and nonstatistical approaches. The documentation requirements do not inherently favor one approach over the other — both require justification of sample design and evaluation of results.
explanations.c: The fundamental distinction between statistical and nonstatistical sampling is that statistical sampling: (1) uses random or systematic selection methods that give each population item a known chance of selection; and (2) applies statistical theory to measure and control sampling risk — providing mathematically quantified confidence levels and projected error rates. Nonstatistical sampling relies on the auditor's professional judgment to select items and evaluate results, which means sampling risk cannot be mathematically quantified. Both approaches can be valid — the choice depends on the auditor's judgment about which provides more persuasive evidence in the circumstances.
explanations.d: Both statistical and nonstatistical sampling can be applied to both tests of controls and tests of details. The sampling approach (statistical vs. nonstatistical) is not determined by the type of test — it is determined by the auditor's judgment about which approach provides more appropriate evidence given the circumstances.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: An auditor is determining the sample size for a test of accounts payable transaction details. Which factors would INCREASE the required sample size?

answers.text: Decreasing the assessed risk of material misstatement or increasing tolerable misstatement
Increasing the assessed risk of material misstatement or decreasing tolerable misstatement
Decreasing the expected error rate and increasing the population size
Decreasing the assessed risk and decreasing tolerable misstatement simultaneously

explanations.a: Decreasing assessed RMM reduces the evidence requirement, leading to smaller samples. Increasing tolerable misstatement (a wider acceptable range) also reduces the sample size needed — less precision is required to conclude within the wider band. Both changes decrease, not increase, the required sample size.
explanations.b: Two factors consistently drive larger sample sizes: (1) Higher assessed risk of material misstatement — when risk is high, more evidence is needed to achieve low detection risk, requiring a larger sample to reach reliable conclusions about the population; (2) Lower tolerable misstatement — when the acceptable threshold is tighter, the auditor needs more precision in the estimate, which requires testing more items. Both factors demand more extensive sampling when they increase or decrease in these directions respectively.
explanations.c: A lower expected error rate tends to reduce sample size (fewer errors are expected, so fewer items need to be tested to detect them). Population size has a relatively minor effect on sample size in most audit sampling contexts — unlike in traditional statistics, the required sample size for large populations does not scale proportionally with population size.
explanations.d: Decreasing both assessed risk and tolerable misstatement simultaneously produces offsetting effects — decreased risk would reduce sample size while decreased tolerable misstatement increases it. The net effect depends on the relative magnitude of each change, and the combination does not consistently lead to increased sample size.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: An auditor tests a sample of 80 accounts payable invoices and finds errors totaling $12,000 in the sample. The population total is $4 million and the sample total was $250,000. Using the ratio projection method, the projected population misstatement is approximately

answers.text: $12,000 — the sample error amount is used directly without projection
$192,000 — the ratio of sample error to sample total, applied to the population total ($12,000 ÷ $250,000 × $4,000,000)
$4,000 — the sample error divided by the sample size (80 items)
$96,000 — 80 divided by 4,000,000 multiplied by 12,000

explanations.a: The sample error amount ($12,000) applies only to the sampled items ($250,000). To reach a conclusion about the full $4 million population, the sample result must be projected to the total — using the sample error alone understates the likely population error and would lead to an incorrect conclusion.
explanations.b: The ratio projection method projects sample misstatements to the population by applying the error ratio found in the sample to the full population: Error ratio = $12,000 ÷ $250,000 = 4.8%; Projected population error = 4.8% × $4,000,000 = $192,000. This projected misstatement is then compared to tolerable misstatement to determine whether the balance appears to be materially misstated.
explanations.c: Dividing the error by the number of items tested ($12,000 ÷ 80 = $150 average error per item) and multiplying by total population items would give a mean-per-unit projection — a different but valid projection method. Dividing by the sample size alone ($4,000) without multiplying by population count is not a valid projection.
explanations.d: The calculation $96,000 = 80 ÷ 4,000,000 × $12,000 is mathematically incorrect as a projection method. This would represent a ratio of population item count to an undefined denominator — it does not represent a recognized audit sampling projection technique.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: An auditor selects a sample of revenue transactions by reviewing the population and choosing items that appear 'representative' — avoiding clustered selections but not using a random number generator. This is BEST described as

answers.text: Statistical sampling — because the auditor applied professional judgment to make it representative
Systematic random sampling — because the selection covered the full population

Haphazard selection — a method of nonstatistical sampling where items are chosen without a systematic pattern, which does not qualify as statistical sampling because each item does not have a known probability of selection
Directed sampling — targeting specific high-risk items rather than drawing from the full population

explanations.a: For sampling to be statistical, items must be selected using a random or systematic method where each population item has a known, non-zero probability of selection. A judgmental selection — even if the auditor believes it is representative — does not give each item a calculable probability of selection and therefore cannot be classified as statistical sampling regardless of the auditor's intent.
explanations.b: Systematic random sampling uses a random start and a fixed interval to select items (e.g., every 50th item). The described method — choosing items that 'appear representative' — is not systematic random sampling; it is judgmental selection without a formal systematic rule.
explanations.c: Haphazard selection involves choosing items without any deliberate pattern — but not using a formal random selection method. While it is used in nonstatistical sampling and attempts to avoid bias, it does not guarantee that each population item has a known probability of selection. Because selection probabilities are unknown, haphazard selection cannot be used to mathematically quantify sampling risk — it is inherently nonstatistical.
explanations.d: Directed sampling (or specific item selection) targets items with specific characteristics (e.g., high-value items, items from a specific vendor) — it is a targeted approach that explicitly focuses on subsets of the population. Haphazard selection from the full population without targeting is different from directed selection.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.keyword: tests of controls and tests of details
questions.text: The PRIMARY purpose of tests of controls is to

answers.text: Determine the exact dollar amount of errors in a financial statement account balance
Obtain evidence that the entity's controls operated effectively throughout the period — supporting the auditor's plan to reduce the extent of substantive procedures
Evaluate whether the financial statement disclosures are complete and properly described
Confirm account balances directly with independent third parties

explanations.a: Tests of controls assess the operating effectiveness of controls — they do not measure the exact dollar amount of errors. The quantity of errors in an account is addressed through tests of details (substantive testing), not tests of controls.
explanations.b: AU-C Section 330 defines tests of controls as audit procedures designed to evaluate the operating effectiveness of controls in preventing, or detecting and correcting, material misstatements at the assertion level. When controls are found to be operating effectively, the auditor can reduce the nature and extent of substantive procedures — relying on the controls to prevent or detect misstatements, rather than independently detecting them through extensive substantive testing.
explanations.c: Evaluating disclosure completeness and accuracy is a substantive procedure — typically performed through procedures such as inquiring of management about required disclosures, reading agreements and contracts, and comparing disclosures to the applicable reporting framework. Tests of controls address the operating effectiveness of processing controls, not the completeness of financial statement disclosures.
explanations.d: Direct confirmation of account balances is a substantive procedure (specifically, a test of details) under AU-C Section 505. Confirmations provide direct external evidence about account balances — a fundamentally different objective than tests of controls.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.keyword: tests of controls and tests of details
questions.text: Under AU-C Section 330, the auditor is REQUIRED to perform tests of controls when

answers.text: The auditor's risk assessment assumes the controls are operating effectively, OR when substantive procedures alone cannot provide sufficient appropriate evidence for a relevant assertion — such as for high-volume automated processes
The entity has an internal audit department that tests controls throughout the year
Management has voluntarily asserted that controls are effective in its annual report
The entity is a publicly traded company subject to SEC reporting requirements

explanations.a: AU-C Section 330 requires tests of controls in two distinct circumstances: (1) when the auditor's risk assessment includes an expectation that controls are operating effectively — if the auditor's substantive testing approach relies on controls to reduce the evidence needed, the auditor must test those controls to confirm they actually operated as expected; and (2) when substantive procedures alone cannot provide sufficient appropriate evidence — this typically applies to highly automated processes where transactions are initiated, processed, and recorded automatically without manual intervention, making substantive testing of individual transactions impractical and leaving the auditor with no alternative to relying on automated controls.
explanations.b: The existence of an internal audit department does not automatically require external auditor tests of controls. The external auditor decides whether to use the work of internal auditors and what additional procedures to perform based on the overall audit strategy — the mere existence of an internal audit function is not a trigger for required tests of controls.
explanations.c: Management's voluntary assertion of control effectiveness does not trigger a required external auditor tests-of-controls requirement for a nonissuer audit. For issuers subject to SOX 404(b), the integrated audit does require the external auditor to independently test and opine on ICFR — but this requirement flows from the statute and PCAOB standards, not from management's assertion alone.
explanations.d: Public company status does require an integrated audit under SOX 404(b) for large accelerated filers and accelerated filers, which includes testing of ICFR. However, this is a more specific condition than simply being publicly traded — not all SEC registrants are subject to the integrated audit requirement.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.keyword: tests of controls and tests of details
questions.text: An auditor selects a sample of accounts payable transactions and for each selected transaction: (1) traces the invoice amount to the supporting purchase order and receiving report to test the three-way match control; and (2) verifies that the invoice amount was accurately recorded in accounts payable. This testing approach is BEST described as

answers.text: Two separate tests — a test of controls performed first, followed by an unrelated substantive test of the same transactions
A test of controls only — since the purpose is to verify whether the control operated correctly
A test of details only — since the primary objective is accuracy of the recorded account balance
A dual-purpose test — simultaneously testing the operating effectiveness of the three-way match control and the accuracy (correctness of amounts) of the recorded accounts payable transactions

explanations.a: While the two objectives (control effectiveness and transaction accuracy) are conceptually distinct, performing them on the same transactions simultaneously is more efficient than two separate tests. This is the design intention of a dual-purpose test — not two sequential unrelated tests.
explanations.b: Characterizing the test as controls-only ignores the substantive component. When the auditor verifies that the invoice amount was accurately recorded, this constitutes substantive testing — it provides direct evidence about the accuracy assertion for the accounts payable balance, not just about whether the control operated.
explanations.c: Characterizing the test as details-only ignores the controls component. When the auditor traces to the purchase order and receiving report to verify the three-way match, this directly tests whether the three-way match control operated correctly — a test of control operating effectiveness.
explanations.d: A dual-purpose test (AU-C 330.A9) simultaneously serves two objectives using the same sample of transactions: (1) it tests whether the control (three-way match) operated effectively — by verifying that purchase orders and receiving reports support each invoice; and (2) it tests whether the accounting entry is accurate — by verifying that the recorded amount matches the invoice. The efficiency of testing both aspects simultaneously is why dual-purpose tests are commonly used in accounts payable, payroll, and revenue testing.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.keyword: tests of controls and tests of details
questions.text: An auditor tests payroll controls at an interim date (September 30) for a December 31 year-end audit. Controls were found to be operating effectively through September 30. What must the auditor do to maintain reliance on these controls through year-end?

answers.text: No further testing is needed — once controls are found effective at interim, they are presumed effective for the full year
Retest the entire payroll control population for the October 1 through December 31 period using the same sample size as the interim test

Perform rollforward procedures for the October through December period — such as inquiring about changes in controls, testing additional transactions from the remaining period, and evaluating whether any changes to the control environment affect the prior conclusion
Report the controls as effective for only the January through September period and perform substantive procedures for October through December as if controls had failed

explanations.a: An interim test that finds controls effective does not automatically extend the conclusion to year-end. AU-C Section 330 requires the auditor to determine whether additional evidence is needed for the remaining period between the interim test date and year-end — the controls must be evaluated for the full period being audited.
explanations.b: Full retesting of the entire population for the remaining period is not required by AU-C 330 — and would be unnecessarily burdensome. Rollforward procedures — which are targeted procedures for the remaining period — are the required approach, not full repetition of the interim test.
explanations.c: AU-C Section 330 requires rollforward procedures when controls are tested at an interim date. Rollforward procedures for the October through December period typically include: (1) inquiring of management about significant changes to controls during the period; (2) reviewing management's own monitoring of controls (internal audit reports, control self-assessments); (3) testing additional transactions from the remaining period, especially if significant changes occurred; and (4) observing whether the factors that led to the conclusion of effective controls at interim (e.g., staffing, IT systems, management oversight) remained in place through year-end.
explanations.d: Treating controls as failed for the remaining period and performing full substantive procedures is not the required response when interim testing was positive. The required approach is targeted rollforward procedures — not treating the interim conclusion as inapplicable.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.keyword: tests of controls and tests of details
questions.text: An auditor tests 60 cash disbursement authorizations and finds 5 exceptions — invoices were approved by personnel who lacked authorization for the amount, resulting in a 8.3% deviation rate. The auditor had established a tolerable deviation rate of 6%. Considering this result, which overall conclusion and response is MOST appropriate?

answers.text: The auditor can still rely on the authorization control since 91.7% of controls operated effectively — the tolerable rate applies only to statistical samples

The 8.3% deviation rate exceeds the 6% tolerable rate — the auditor cannot rely on this control; substantive testing of accounts payable must be expanded, and the control deficiency must be evaluated for communication to management and TCWG and assessed as a possible significant deficiency or material weakness
The auditor should increase the sample size to 120 items to determine if the additional testing reduces the projected deviation rate below 6%
The auditor should negotiate with management to increase the tolerable deviation rate to 9% to accommodate the finding

explanations.a: The tolerable deviation rate applies to the auditor's conclusion about the population from which the sample was drawn — regardless of whether statistical or nonstatistical sampling was used. A deviation rate of 8.3% that exceeds 6% tolerable means the auditor cannot rely on the control to be operating effectively at an acceptable level. The 91.7% compliance rate means approximately 8.3% of authorization decisions in the population may have been improperly authorized — an unacceptable control failure rate.
explanations.b: This is the correct multi-part response. When the sample deviation rate exceeds the tolerable rate, the auditor must: (1) conclude that the control cannot be relied upon — the auditor's plan to reduce substantive procedures based on this control is invalidated; (2) expand substantive testing of accounts payable to compensate for the inability to rely on the authorization control — the substantive work must directly test whether payments were for authorized, legitimate obligations; (3) evaluate the nature of the exceptions — were they all from one department, one approver, one period? Understanding the pattern helps assess severity; (4) communicate the control deficiency to management and TCWG, as required by AU-C 265; and (5) evaluate whether the deficiency constitutes a significant deficiency or material weakness given the rate and nature of exceptions.
explanations.c: Expanding the sample after finding a deviation rate above the tolerable rate may refine the estimate of the population deviation rate — but if the extended sample still shows a rate above tolerable, the same conclusion applies. Expanding the sample to 'hope for better results' is not an appropriate professional response if the original sample was properly designed.
explanations.d: Tolerable deviation rates are set based on the auditor's assessment of how much deviation can be accepted while still relying on the control — they are not negotiable with management. A tolerable rate reflects the auditor's professional judgment about what level of control failure is acceptable; it cannot be arbitrarily increased to accommodate inconvenient test results.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: Analytical procedures, as defined in AU-C Section 520, involve

answers.text: Confirming individual account balances directly with independent external parties to verify their accuracy
Physically counting and inspecting assets to verify their existence at the balance sheet date
Recalculating amounts in the financial statements to verify their mathematical accuracy

Evaluating financial information by studying plausible relationships among both financial and non-financial data — including comparisons with prior periods, industry benchmarks, budgets, and reasonableness estimates based on the auditor's understanding of the entity

explanations.a: Confirming account balances with independent external parties is the confirmation procedure described in AU-C Section 505 — a test of details, not an analytical procedure.
explanations.b: Physically counting and inspecting assets is an observation and inspection procedure — a direct test of existence — not an analytical procedure.
explanations.c: Recalculating amounts tests mathematical accuracy through the auditor's own computation — it is the recalculation procedure described in AU-C 500.A21, not an analytical procedure.
explanations.d: AU-C Section 520 defines analytical procedures as evaluations of financial information by studying plausible relationships among both financial and non-financial data. Examples include: comparing current-year revenue growth to prior periods and industry trends; testing the relationship between headcount changes and payroll expense changes; using regression analysis to predict expected utility expense based on production levels; and comparing gross margin percentages across periods. Analytical procedures are used at planning, as substantive procedures, and at the completion phase of the audit.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: For substantive analytical procedures to provide meaningful evidence, the auditor must develop an independent expectation BEFORE comparing it to the recorded amount. This requirement exists because

answers.text: Developing the expectation after seeing the recorded amount ensures the comparison is more accurate since the auditor can calibrate the expectation to match
Professional standards require a three-step documentation process that begins with the expectation — a documentation requirement, not an evidential requirement

An expectation developed after seeing the recorded amount would be influenced by that amount — defeating the independent analytical comparison; the expectation must be independently derived to detect whether the recorded amount is plausible
The expectation is disclosed to management before fieldwork to allow them to correct any errors proactively

explanations.a: Developing an expectation after seeing the recorded amount — and then 'calibrating' it to match — would circular. If the expectation is anchored to what management reported, the comparison provides no independent evidence about whether the recorded amount is reasonable. The expectation must be developed from independent sources and reasoning before the recorded amount is observed.
explanations.b: Documentation requirements are important, but they are not the primary rationale for developing an independent expectation. The evidential rationale — preventing the expectation from being influenced by the recorded amount — is the fundamental reason for the requirement.
explanations.c: When the auditor develops an expectation before looking at the recorded amount, the comparison between the expectation and the recorded amount is genuinely independent — any significant difference represents a real discrepancy that requires explanation. If the expectation were developed after seeing the recorded amount, it would naturally gravitate toward the recorded amount (the anchoring effect), eliminating the analytical procedure's power to detect potential misstatements. An expectation developed from independent data (prior periods, industry rates, non-financial drivers like units sold) that is then compared to the recorded amount provides meaningful evidence when they correspond — or a meaningful red flag when they do not.
explanations.d: Disclosing the expectation to management before fieldwork is not a standard practice. The expectation is the auditor's independent analytical tool — it is not shared with management as a proactive correction mechanism.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: An auditor develops an expectation for sales commissions expense of approximately $2.1 million based on 8% of recorded revenue of $26.3 million. The entity's recorded commissions expense is $3.6 million — $1.5 million more than the expectation. Management explains the difference as 'special commissions paid on a large new customer contract.' How should the auditor respond?

answers.text: Accept management's explanation since special commissions are a plausible business explanation for an unusual amount
Reduce the expected commission rate to match the recorded amount and document that analytical procedures were completed
Treat the $1.5 million difference as a confirmed misstatement and immediately propose an audit adjustment

Investigate the explanation by obtaining and reviewing the specific contract that generated the special commissions, verifying the commission terms, confirming the payment amount, and assessing whether the explanation is corroborated by objective evidence before concluding

explanations.a: Management's explanation is plausible — but plausibility is not corroboration. The purpose of analytical procedures is to identify significant differences that require explanation; when a difference is found, the auditor must evaluate whether the explanation is supported by objective evidence, not merely accept it because it sounds reasonable. An unsupported explanation is no better than no explanation for evidential purposes.
explanations.b: Adjusting the expectation retroactively to match the recorded amount — and then documenting 'analytical procedures were completed' — is not a valid audit approach. This would eliminate the analytical procedure's evidential value entirely and would constitute misrepresentation of the work performed.
explanations.c: The analytical difference does not automatically mean a misstatement — it means the relationship between revenue and commissions was different from expected. If management's explanation (a special commission on a large new contract) is legitimate and supported by documentation, the higher amount may be accurately recorded. The analytical difference requires investigation, not automatic treatment as a misstatement.
explanations.d: AU-C Section 520 requires the auditor to investigate significant and unexpected differences in analytical procedures. When management provides an explanation, the auditor must evaluate whether it is plausible AND corroborated. For a $1.5 million difference: (1) obtain and review the specific contract that purportedly generated the special commission — verify the commission terms, the commission rate, and the payment triggers; (2) confirm the amount paid to the sales representative or agent; (3) assess whether the commission amount is proportionate to the contract value; and (4) determine whether the explanation is fully supported or whether additional investigation is needed.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: At the completion of an audit, the engagement partner performs a final review of the financial statements using analytical procedures and notices that the entity's gross margin has declined from 42% in the prior year to 31% in the current year — a change not explained by previously identified and resolved matters. Field work has been substantially completed. Which response is MOST appropriate?

answers.text: Issue the audit report as planned since field work has been completed and the gross margin change may be explained by competitive pricing pressure

Evaluate whether the unexplained gross margin decline — which represents a potentially significant change in the relationship between revenue and cost of goods sold — indicates a possible undetected misstatement requiring additional procedures before the report is issued
Reduce the audit opinion from unmodified to qualified based solely on the unexplained gross margin decline
Disclose the gross margin decline in an emphasis-of-matter paragraph as an unexplained matter

explanations.a: Issuing the report without investigating an unexplained significant analytical finding is a fundamental failure of the final review process. The final review analytics are specifically designed to identify issues that may have been missed during field work — an unexplained significant change must be investigated, not rationalized as possibly explained by unverified factors.
explanations.b: AU-C Section 520 requires the auditor to perform analytical procedures at or near the end of the audit to assist in forming an overall conclusion about whether the financial statements are consistent with the auditor's understanding of the entity. The gross margin decline from 42% to 31% is a significant change that would affect user decisions and should have been identified and explained during the audit. If it was not identified and explained during field work, it may indicate: a misstatement in revenue (overstatement) or cost of goods sold (understatement); an inventory issue; or a real business change that was not considered in the audit approach.
