The engagement partner must investigate before issuing the report — this may require additional procedures even though field work has been substantially completed.
explanations.c: Issuing a qualified opinion based solely on an unexplained analytical finding — without identifying an actual misstatement — is inappropriate. A qualified opinion is issued because of a specific identified matter (a misstatement or scope limitation), not because of an unexplained analytical result. Investigation may determine that the change is real and properly accounted for, resolving the concern.
explanations.d: An emphasis-of-matter paragraph draws attention to information already presented in the financial statements — it is not used to flag the auditor's own unresolved analytical findings. The analytical concern must be resolved (either explained and supported, or identified as indicating a misstatement) before the report is issued.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: How does a positive confirmation request differ from a negative confirmation request?

answers.text: A positive confirmation is sent to all customers regardless of balance size; a negative confirmation is sent only to customers with balances above a specified threshold
A positive confirmation requires the recipient to return it within 10 days; a negative confirmation allows 30 days for response

A positive confirmation requests the recipient to respond whether they agree or disagree with the stated balance; a negative confirmation requests a response ONLY if the recipient disagrees with the information — no response implies agreement
A positive confirmation is sent via certified mail; a negative confirmation is sent via email

explanations.a: AU-C Section 505 does not define positive and negative confirmations based on balance-size thresholds. The distinction is about what type of response is requested from the recipient — not the size criterion for selection.
explanations.b: Timing requirements for confirmation responses are not what distinguishes positive from negative confirmations. There is no standard mandated response period in AU-C 505 — the form of response requested is the defining characteristic.
explanations.c: AU-C Section 505 defines the two forms of confirmation: (1) Positive confirmation — a request that the recipient respond directly to the auditor, indicating whether they agree or disagree with the information in the confirmation request (a response is requested regardless of the recipient's agreement); and (2) Negative confirmation — a request that the recipient respond directly to the auditor only if the recipient disagrees with the stated information. If no response is received, the auditor treats it as implicit agreement. Negative confirmations provide less reliable evidence because non-response may reflect indifference rather than agreement.
explanations.d: The delivery method (certified mail vs. email) does not define positive vs. negative confirmations. Either form can be sent by any medium — the defining characteristic is whether a response is requested regardless of agreement (positive) or only if there is disagreement (negative).

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: AU-C Section 505 requires the auditor to use external confirmation procedures for accounts receivable unless certain conditions are present. Which condition would permit the auditor to OMIT confirmations for accounts receivable?

answers.text: The accounts receivable balance is immaterial, prior experience indicates confirmations will be ineffective (e.g., very low response rates), or substantive analytical procedures combined with other procedures would provide sufficient appropriate evidence
The entity has an active internal audit function that has already confirmed the receivables balances
Management has requested that confirmations not be sent due to potential disruption to customer relationships
The auditor is performing a review engagement rather than an audit engagement for accounts receivable

explanations.a: AU-C Section 505.09 provides three circumstances under which confirmation of accounts receivable is not required: (1) the overall receivable balance is immaterial — if the balance does not affect the financial statements materially, the cost of confirmation is disproportionate to the benefit; (2) the auditor has determined that confirmations would be ineffective — for example, if prior years had very low response rates or frequent exceptions that were difficult to resolve, making the procedure unreliable as evidence; or (3) the auditor's risk assessment is sufficiently low and analytical procedures combined with other procedures (testing subsequent receipts, examining shipping documents) would provide sufficient appropriate evidence.
explanations.b: The existence of an internal audit function that performed confirmations does not permit the external auditor to omit this procedure. External auditors may use the work of internal auditors in some circumstances, but internal audit confirmations do not substitute for the external auditor's own confirmation procedures — they lack the direct independent nature of external confirmations sent by the external auditor.
explanations.c: Management's request to omit confirmations due to customer relationship concerns is a management-imposed scope limitation — not a recognized exception in AU-C 505. If the auditor agrees to management's restriction without an acceptable alternative, the auditor has a scope limitation that must be evaluated for its effect on the audit opinion.
explanations.d: Review engagements under SSARS or PCAOB AS 4105 are separate from audit engagements and have different procedures — but this does not create an exception to confirmation requirements within an audit engagement. The question concerns when confirmations can be omitted in an audit.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: An auditor sends positive confirmation requests to 45 customers. After two follow-up attempts, 8 customers have not responded. The auditor's MOST appropriate response to the non-responses is to

answers.text: Treat the non-responses as implicit agreement with the stated balances — non-response to a positive confirmation is equivalent to a 'no exceptions' response
Reduce the assessed reliability of the confirmation evidence proportionally by 17.8% to account for the non-respondents
Issue a qualified opinion because non-responses indicate that customers may dispute those balances

Perform alternative procedures on the non-responding accounts — such as examining subsequent cash receipts, reviewing shipping documentation, and inspecting other evidence supporting the receivable balances — to obtain sufficient appropriate evidence for those items

explanations.a: Non-response to a positive confirmation is NOT treated as agreement — it is a significant limitation on the evidence. Positive confirmations specifically require a direct response regardless of agreement; the absence of a response means the auditor has not obtained any independent confirmation of those balances. This treatment applies to negative confirmations (where non-response implies agreement), not positive confirmations.
explanations.b: Proportional reliability reduction is not a recognized methodology for addressing non-responses. Non-responses represent a complete absence of confirmation evidence for those accounts — they require alternative procedures to obtain the needed evidence, not mathematical adjustment to the overall reliability estimate.
explanations.c: Non-responses do not indicate customer disputes — they indicate non-participation. Customers may not respond for many reasons (changed addresses, administrative delays, disinterest). A qualified opinion requires actual evidence of a misstatement or scope limitation — non-response alone, before alternative procedures are applied, does not rise to that level.
explanations.d: AU-C Section 505.12 requires the auditor to perform alternative procedures on positive confirmations that receive no response. Alternative procedures provide evidence about the same assertions that the confirmation was designed to address — principally existence and accuracy of the receivable. Effective alternative procedures include: examining subsequent cash receipts (verifying the customer paid after year-end, corroborating the balance's existence and collectability); inspecting shipping documents and customer purchase orders for the specific transactions; and examining sales contracts.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: An auditor sends a positive confirmation to Customer Z for a balance of $312,000. Customer Z responds that it recognizes only $247,000 — noting that a $65,000 invoice is disputed because the goods were allegedly defective. Management insists the goods were conforming and the full balance is collectible. How should the auditor evaluate this confirmation exception?

answers.text: Accept management's position since management has direct knowledge of the product quality and the customer's response does not constitute audit evidence

Investigate the $65,000 difference by examining the relevant invoice and shipping documentation, reviewing any customer complaints or return requests, evaluating the collectability of the disputed amount, and assessing whether a provision may be needed
Treat the entire $312,000 balance as uncollectible since the customer has disputed a portion
Request a second confirmation from Customer Z since the first response may have been made in error

explanations.a: Customer Z's response constitutes independent external evidence — it is precisely the type of evidence that confirmations are designed to provide. Dismissing it because management disagrees would ignore the confirmation's evidentiary purpose. Management's assertions are less reliable than independent customer responses.
explanations.b: AU-C Section 505 requires the auditor to investigate exceptions (differences between confirmed amounts and recorded amounts). For the $65,000 disputed invoice, the auditor should: (1) examine the invoice — verifying the description of goods, price, and shipment date; (2) review shipping documentation to confirm delivery occurred; (3) investigate whether the customer filed a formal quality complaint or return request, which would corroborate their claim; (4) evaluate collectability — if the dispute is legitimate, a provision may be required; (5) consider whether the dispute indicates an inaccuracy in recorded revenue or receivables. The investigation may ultimately support either management's position or the customer's position, depending on the objective evidence found.
explanations.c: A disputed invoice does not mean the entire balance is uncollectible. The customer acknowledges $247,000 — only the $65,000 disputed invoice is in question. The auditor must investigate the specific disputed amount without impacting the undisputed portion.
explanations.d: Requesting a second confirmation to see if Customer Z changes their response is not an appropriate investigative procedure. If the customer's first response was based on a genuine dispute or error, the auditor should investigate the underlying facts rather than hoping for a different response.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: Management informs the auditor that confirmations should NOT be sent to two specific major customers — who together account for 42% of total accounts receivable — because 'those relationships are sensitive and confirmations could jeopardize the business.' The auditor has no prior experience that suggests confirmations to these customers would be ineffective. Which assessment is MOST appropriate?

answers.text: The auditor should honor management's request — protecting business relationships is a legitimate operational concern that justifies omitting confirmations for these customers
The auditor should reduce the confirmation sample to exclude these two customers and compensate by confirming additional smaller-balance customers

Management's request is a scope limitation — the auditor should consider why management is restricting the procedure, evaluate whether alternative procedures can provide sufficient appropriate evidence for the 42% of receivables at issue, and if not, consider the effect on the audit opinion — including a possible qualified opinion or disclaimer
The auditor should send confirmations to these customers without informing management, since the auditor controls the confirmation process

explanations.a: Management's business relationship concern does not constitute a recognized exception to the confirmation requirement under AU-C 505. Unlike the recognized exceptions (immaterial balance, ineffective procedure, sufficient alternative evidence), a client's reluctance to allow confirmations due to relationship concerns is a scope limitation — and one that may itself indicate a red flag if management is particularly resistant to independent third-party corroboration of a significant receivable balance.
explanations.b: Replacing the two major customers (42% of receivables) with additional small-balance customers does not address the same population. The receivable balance for these two customers remains untested by confirmation. Adding more small-balance confirmations does not provide evidence about the large-balance accounts excluded from the process.
explanations.c: AU-C Section 505 treats management-imposed restrictions on the confirmation process as scope limitations — similar to restrictions on any other audit procedure. When management imposes such restrictions, the auditor must: (1) investigate the reasons — restrictions on independent evidence gathering can themselves be fraud risk indicators; (2) evaluate whether alternative procedures (subsequent receipts examination, contract review, shipping document inspection) can provide sufficient appropriate evidence for the restricted accounts; and (3) if alternative procedures cannot provide sufficient evidence, evaluate whether the inability to confirm 42% of accounts receivable creates a material scope limitation that requires a modified opinion.
explanations.d: While the auditor controls the confirmation process (selecting recipients and mailing directly), secretly sending confirmations contrary to management's explicit instructions would damage the client relationship and potentially create legal issues. The professional response is to evaluate the restriction and its implications — not to circumvent it unilaterally.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: AU-C Section 540 identifies three general approaches an auditor may use when auditing accounting estimates. Which of the following correctly identifies these three approaches?

answers.text: Testing controls, performing substantive procedures, and issuing management letters
Inquiry, inspection, and observation
Analytical procedures, tests of details, and tests of controls

Testing management's process for developing the estimate; developing an independent estimate to compare to management's; and reviewing subsequent events or transactions that provide evidence about the estimate

explanations.a: Testing controls, performing substantive procedures, and issuing management letters are categories of audit engagement activities — not the three specific approaches to auditing accounting estimates under AU-C 540.
explanations.b: Inquiry, inspection, and observation are audit evidence-gathering techniques that may be used within any of the three approaches — they are not the three approaches themselves.
explanations.c: Analytical procedures, tests of details, and tests of controls are broad categories of audit procedures. While they may be applied within an approach to auditing estimates, they are not the three approaches specified in AU-C 540 for estimates.
explanations.d: AU-C Section 540 specifies three approaches for auditing accounting estimates: (1) Test management's process — evaluate the reasonableness of the assumptions, the quality of the data inputs, and the appropriateness of the estimation methodology; (2) Develop an independent estimate — construct the auditor's own estimate of the amount and compare it to management's estimate to assess whether management's is within a reasonable range; and (3) Review subsequent events or transactions — examine events or transactions that occur after the balance sheet date but before the audit report date, which may provide evidence that either corroborates or contradicts the estimate. The auditor selects the approach(es) appropriate to the specific estimate.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: When testing management's process for developing an accounting estimate, the auditor's procedures MOST commonly include

answers.text: Evaluating the completeness and accuracy of data inputs, assessing the reasonableness of significant assumptions, determining whether the estimation method is appropriate for the applicable reporting framework, and identifying whether any changes in the estimation approach are properly supported
Replacing management's estimate entirely with the auditor's own independently derived estimate
Requiring management to hire a certified specialist to prepare all estimates above a specified dollar threshold
Confirming the estimate with management's external legal counsel to obtain independent corroboration

explanations.a: Testing management's process under AU-C 540 involves evaluating each component of the estimation process: (1) Data inputs — are the inputs complete, accurate, and relevant? For example, for an allowance for doubtful accounts, does the historical write-off rate data include all relevant periods without cherry-picking favorable periods?; (2) Assumptions — are significant assumptions (e.g., recovery rates, discount rates, growth rates) internally consistent, supported by market data, and unbiased?; (3) Estimation method — is the method appropriate for the type of estimate and consistent with the applicable reporting framework (e.g., CECL for credit losses)?; and (4) Changes in approach — if management changed the estimation methodology from the prior year, is the change appropriately justified and disclosed?
explanations.b: Developing an independent estimate is a separate approach under AU-C 540 — not part of testing management's process. When testing management's process, the auditor evaluates what management did — not replaces it.
explanations.c: Management's decision to use certified specialists is a management choice. The auditor evaluates whether specialist involvement is appropriate and whether the specialist's qualifications are adequate — but the auditor cannot require management to hire specialists for all estimates above a threshold.
explanations.d: External legal counsel provides letters about legal matters — they do not corroborate accounting estimates such as fair values, allowances, or warranty reserves. The appropriate independent corroboration for estimates comes from market data, specialist opinions, or subsequent outcomes — not legal counsel.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: A retrospective review reveals that management's allowance for doubtful accounts estimate has been consistently 30-40% below actual write-off experience for the past three years. How should this finding affect the audit of the current-year estimate?

answers.text: The pattern is irrelevant since each year's estimate should be evaluated independently based on current-year conditions
The pattern constitutes conclusive evidence of fraud — the auditor must immediately withdraw from the engagement and report to law enforcement
The auditor should accept management's estimate but increase the overall materiality threshold for accounts receivable to compensate for the historical understatement

The consistent pattern of underestimation is an indicator of management bias — the auditor should apply heightened skepticism, challenge management's current assumptions more rigorously, consider whether an upward adjustment is warranted, and evaluate whether the pattern reflects intentional understatement of the allowance

explanations.a: Prior-period retrospective review results are directly relevant to evaluating current-period estimates. AU-C 540 requires the auditor to perform retrospective reviews of prior-period estimates specifically to inform the assessment of management's current-period estimation process and to identify potential management bias.
explanations.b: A consistent underestimation pattern is a risk indicator — not conclusive evidence of fraud. It requires investigation and heightened skepticism, not automatic withdrawal. The pattern may reflect consistently optimistic but honest assumptions, or it may indicate intentional understatement — determining which requires further investigation.
explanations.c: Increasing materiality to compensate for a historical pattern of understatement is inappropriate — it would reduce audit scrutiny in an area already identified as having a bias pattern. Materiality is set based on user information needs, not calibrated to accommodate management's estimation patterns.
explanations.d: A consistent pattern of underestimating an allowance by 30-40% over three years is a significant indicator of management bias in the estimation process. AU-C 540 requires the auditor to evaluate whether identified differences between management's estimates and actual outcomes indicate management bias. Consistent optimistic estimation (understating the allowance) suggests management may be intentionally or systematically making favorable assumptions. The auditor should: apply heightened skepticism to current-year assumptions; independently evaluate the key drivers (e.g., historical loss rates by aging bucket, current economic conditions, specific large delinquent accounts); consider whether an adjustment to the current estimate is necessary; and evaluate whether the pattern rises to the level of a fraud risk indicator.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: An entity holds significant investments in private equity funds that have no quoted market prices. Management has valued these investments using a discounted cash flow (DCF) model with internally developed assumptions about growth rates and discount rates. Why do Level 3 fair value measurements like this require more extensive audit procedures than Level 1 measurements?

answers.text: Level 3 measurements require more procedures because they involve more transactions than Level 1 measurements
Level 3 measurements require the same procedures as Level 1 — the level classification is an accounting disclosure requirement, not a risk factor that affects the audit approach

Level 3 measurements use significant unobservable inputs based on management's assumptions — which cannot be independently corroborated from market prices, making the audit more reliant on evaluating the reasonableness of those assumptions and increasing susceptibility to management bias
Level 3 measurements require more procedures only when the investment exceeds a specified dollar threshold set by the FASB

explanations.a: The volume of transactions is not what distinguishes Level 3 from Level 1 in terms of audit complexity. A single Level 3 investment can require extensive audit procedures, while thousands of Level 1 investments with quoted prices can be tested efficiently using market price sources.
explanations.b: The fair value level classification (ASC 820) directly affects audit risk assessment. Level 1 measurements use unadjusted quoted prices in active markets — the auditor simply looks up the market price. Level 3 measurements use significant unobservable inputs — management's own assumptions — which have no independent external benchmark, creating significantly higher estimation uncertainty and audit risk.
explanations.c: The key audit challenge with Level 3 measurements is that the inputs — growth rate projections, discount rates, terminal values, probability weightings — are developed internally by management and cannot be directly verified from observable market data. The auditor cannot simply 'look up' the fair value; instead, they must evaluate the reasonableness of management's assumptions, the appropriateness of the model, and whether the overall estimate falls within a reasonable range. This creates greater susceptibility to management bias (optimistic assumptions that inflate valuations) and requires more extensive procedures, often including a valuation specialist.
explanations.d: No dollar threshold set by the FASB or any auditing standard determines when Level 3 measurements require more procedures. The level of audit effort is determined by the auditor's risk assessment — high estimation uncertainty from Level 3 inputs increases audit risk regardless of the dollar amount involved.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: An auditor engages a valuation specialist to independently evaluate management's goodwill impairment assessment. The specialist concludes that a reasonable range for the fair value of the reporting unit is $8.5 million to $10.2 million. Management's estimated fair value is $12.1 million — above the range — and therefore management concludes no impairment exists (the carrying value is $10.0 million). Management provides detailed support for its specific assumptions. How should the auditor evaluate this situation?

answers.text: Accept management's estimate since they have provided detailed support for their specific assumptions — the specialist's range is one opinion and management's detailed analysis is another
Accept management's estimate if it is higher than the specialist's range — management's internal knowledge of the business always provides more reliable estimates than external specialists

The auditor must evaluate whether management's assumptions are reasonable and whether the $12.1 million estimate is supportable; since the estimate exceeds the specialist's independently derived range, the auditor should challenge management's assumptions, assess whether they represent management bias, and consider whether an adjustment is required — and if management declines to adjust and the difference is material, the auditor should consider modifying the opinion
Automatically issue an adverse opinion since management's estimate falls outside the specialist's range

explanations.a: Providing detailed support for assumptions is not sufficient to override an independent evaluation that places the estimate outside a reasonable range. The auditor must evaluate whether management's specific assumptions are actually reasonable — detailed documentation supporting an unreasonable assumption does not make the assumption acceptable.
explanations.b: Management's internal knowledge of the business is relevant context but does not automatically produce more reliable estimates than an independent specialist. The purpose of engaging a specialist is precisely to obtain an independent view that counterbalances potential management bias. If management consistently produced more reliable fair value estimates than specialists, engaging specialists would provide no incremental benefit.
explanations.c: When management's estimate falls outside the auditor's independently derived reasonable range (the specialist's range of $8.5M-$10.2M), this is a significant finding. The auditor must: (1) understand and critically evaluate the specific assumptions that drive management's higher estimate; (2) assess whether those assumptions are reasonable given current market conditions and company performance; (3) determine whether the differences in assumptions reflect legitimate business judgment or management bias to avoid recording an impairment; (4) consider that if the carrying value ($10.0M) falls within or below the specialist's range, an impairment may exist — management's $12.1M estimate avoids impairment while the specialist's range would result in impairment; and (5) if the auditor cannot accept management's estimate and management refuses to adjust, evaluate the materiality of the difference and consider a modified opinion.
explanations.d: An adverse opinion requires that the financial statements are materially misstated — which means the auditor must reach a conclusion that management's estimate is wrong and that a material misstatement exists. Before issuing an adverse opinion, the auditor must complete the investigation and discussion with management. Additionally, if management adjusts to within the acceptable range, no opinion modification is needed.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: To verify the existence of investment securities held by the entity, the auditor should MOST commonly

answers.text: Inspect the security certificates or obtain direct confirmation from the broker-dealer, custodian, or third-party depository holding the securities on behalf of the entity
Review the entity's investment policy to confirm it authorizes the specific types of securities held
Obtain representations from management that all listed investments exist and are properly recorded
Compare the investment balances to published industry averages for similar entities

explanations.a: AU-C Section 501 addresses the auditor's procedures for investments, including verifying existence. The most direct procedures for existence include: (1) physically inspecting the actual security certificates when held by the entity; (2) obtaining positive confirmation from the broker-dealer, custodian, or clearing organization (such as DTCC) that holds the securities on the entity's behalf — these third-party confirmations provide independent external evidence of existence; and (3) for securities registered in the entity's name, reviewing transfer agent records. These procedures directly corroborate the existence of the securities independent of entity records.
explanations.b: The investment policy establishes authorization parameters — it does not corroborate the existence of specific securities. An entity could hold securities that conform to its investment policy but that don't actually exist in the accounts as described.
explanations.c: Management representations are the least reliable evidence for existence — if management is misrepresenting investments, their representations would also be false. The existence assertion specifically requires independent external corroboration, which confirmations from custodians or inspection of certificates provide.
explanations.d: Comparing to industry averages addresses plausibility at a high level — it is an analytical procedure that might identify unreasonable balances but does not provide direct evidence of existence for the specific investments recorded.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: An entity holds publicly traded equity securities measured at fair value through net income under ASC 321. The audit procedures for the valuation of these securities MOST commonly involve

answers.text: Engaging a valuation specialist to independently appraise each security since all equity securities require specialist involvement
Testing internal controls over the investment accounting process since effective controls provide sufficient evidence of fair value accuracy

Obtaining the quoted market prices from an independent pricing source as of the measurement date and verifying the entity applied the correct price to the correct quantity of shares to compute the fair value
Confirming the securities' fair values with the entity's investment advisor who selected the securities

explanations.a: Specialist involvement is generally not required for Level 1 securities (publicly traded equity securities with quoted prices in active markets). Specialist involvement is more appropriate for Level 2 and Level 3 measurements where observable inputs are limited or absent. Using a specialist for publicly quoted securities would be disproportionate to the audit risk.
explanations.b: Tests of controls, even when effective, are not sufficient alone for the valuation assertion of investment securities. AU-C 330 requires substantive procedures for all significant accounts regardless of control assessment — the auditor must directly verify the fair values through substantive testing.
explanations.c: For publicly traded equity securities (Level 1 fair value measurements under ASC 820), the valuation procedure is straightforward: (1) obtain the closing market price on the measurement date from an independent external pricing source (such as a financial data service, not management's records); (2) verify the entity applied the correct price; and (3) confirm the quantity of shares owned. The product of price × quantity equals the fair value. The independent external price source provides highly reliable evidence for Level 1 measurements.
explanations.d: The investment advisor's confirmation of fair values is not independent — the advisor works for the entity's benefit and may have incentives to confirm valuations favorably. Independent pricing services (market data providers) provide more objective evidence of market prices than the entity's own investment advisor.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: An entity classifies a portfolio of corporate bonds as held-to-maturity (HTM) under ASC 320, measuring them at amortized cost. When evaluating management's HTM classification, the auditor MOST directly assesses

answers.text: Whether the market values of the bonds exceed their amortized cost, which would indicate the HTM classification is advantageous

Whether management has both the positive intent to hold the securities to maturity AND the financial ability to do so — based on evidence such as the entity's investment policies, past practices with similar investments, and current liquidity position
Whether the bond issuers have investment-grade credit ratings from recognized rating agencies
Whether management consulted with external auditors before making the classification decision in the prior year

explanations.a: The relationship between market value and amortized cost indicates whether unrealized gains or losses exist — it is relevant to whether the entity might have economic motivation to reclassify, but it does not directly address whether management has the intent and ability to hold to maturity. The HTM classification is not justified or invalidated by the current market price relationship.
explanations.b: ASC 320 requires HTM classification only when the entity has both the positive intent AND the financial ability to hold the investments to maturity. The auditor evaluates both elements: (1) Intent — does the entity's investment policy specify HTM, and has the entity historically held similar bonds to maturity without early disposal?; (2) Ability — does the entity have sufficient liquidity and financial resources to hold the bonds without needing to sell them before maturity (e.g., to meet cash flow needs)? If the entity faces liquidity pressures, the financial ability to hold may be in question. Inappropriate HTM classification would require measurement at fair value instead of amortized cost.
explanations.c: Credit ratings of bond issuers are relevant to evaluating collectability and impairment risk — not to evaluating the HTM classification decision. The HTM classification depends on the entity's intent and ability, not the issuer's credit quality.
explanations.d: Consulting with prior-year auditors before making accounting classifications is not a GAAP requirement, and whether it occurred has no bearing on whether the current-year classification is appropriate.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: An entity holds interests in several private investment funds (Level 3 fair values). Management has used the Net Asset Value (NAV) practical expedient under ASC 820 for one fund and internally modeled DCF valuations for two others. The auditor's evaluation of these investments should MOST focus on

answers.text: Whether the investment advisor's management fees are within market rates for the relevant fund types
Whether the entity has complied with the legal requirements for investing in private funds under securities regulations
Whether the disclosures in the footnotes identify the Level 3 designation — which is the auditor's primary responsibility for complex investments

For the NAV investment: whether the NAV practical expedient qualifies (no active redemption restrictions) and whether the NAV used is current; for the DCF investments: whether the models, assumptions (discount rates, growth rates), and inputs are reasonable, and whether engaging a specialist would provide more persuasive evidence

explanations.a: Management fee reasonableness is a business economic consideration — it does not address the valuation assertions for the investment balances. The auditor's focus for investments is on existence, completeness, valuation, and proper classification/disclosure.
explanations.b: Legal compliance with securities regulations is a compliance matter — it does not directly address whether the investments are fairly valued in the financial statements. The auditor considers legal matters separately under AU-C 250.
explanations.c: While disclosure completeness (including the Level 3 designation) is important, it is one aspect of the audit — not the primary focus for complex investment valuation. The more challenging aspect is evaluating whether the recorded values are reasonable, which requires testing the underlying valuation approaches.
explanations.d: The audit approach for these two types of Level 3 investments differs based on the methodology used: (1) NAV practical expedient — the auditor verifies eligibility (the fund is not restricted from redemption at NAV, meaning NAV is a meaningful price proxy) and obtains current, complete NAV information from the fund administrator, confirming it was calculated consistent with ASC 946 (Investment Company guidance); (2) DCF models — the auditor (potentially with a valuation specialist) evaluates the model structure, tests the reasonableness of key assumptions (discount rates against market benchmarks, growth rates against industry data), verifies input data quality, and considers whether the overall valuation falls within a reasonable range. Given the complexity and risk of bias in Level 3 DCF valuations, involving a specialist is often warranted.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.keyword: inventory and inventory held by others
questions.text: AU-C Section 501 requires the auditor to observe the physical inventory count when inventory is material, unless

answers.text: Management requests that the auditor not be present during the physical count to avoid disrupting operations

Physical inventory observation is impractical — for example, when the auditor was not engaged until after the physical count date — in which case the auditor must perform alternative procedures to obtain sufficient evidence about inventory quantities
The entity uses a perpetual inventory system that is updated in real time, which makes physical observation redundant
The entity's inventory is held in a public warehouse, making observation the responsibility of the warehouse operator

explanations.a: Management's preference not to have the auditor present during the count is a management-imposed scope limitation — not a recognized exception to the observation requirement. If the auditor accepts this restriction without alternative procedures, they may face a scope limitation affecting the opinion.
explanations.b: AU-C Section 501.07 recognizes that in some circumstances, observation of the physical inventory count may be impractical — most commonly when the auditor is engaged after the physical count has already been performed. In such cases, the auditor must perform alternative procedures — such as examining evidence of the count (count sheets, pre-numbered count tags), performing a subsequent count and tracing changes back to the year-end balance, or evaluating perpetual records and their reconciliation to the year-end count. If alternative procedures cannot provide sufficient evidence, the auditor considers the effect on the opinion.
explanations.c: A perpetual inventory system does not eliminate the need for physical observation. Perpetual records are only as reliable as the underlying counts and transaction processing. Physical observation provides evidence about the existence of inventory and the effectiveness of counting procedures — evidence that a perpetual system's records alone cannot provide.
explanations.d: Inventory held in a public warehouse is inventory belonging to the entity that the auditor still needs to verify. The warehouse operator's records are management-provided evidence and must be independently corroborated — typically by confirmation from the warehouse or, for material amounts, a visit to the warehouse for physical observation.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.keyword: inventory and inventory held by others
questions.text: To test the accuracy of inventory cutoff at December 31, an auditor records the last 10 shipping document numbers used before year-end and the first 10 numbers used in January. Which subsequent procedure MOST directly tests whether cutoff was applied correctly?

answers.text: Confirming the inventory quantities with the entity's major suppliers to verify that shipments recorded were actually made
Reviewing the entity's inventory count sheets to determine whether all items were counted during the physical inventory
Performing analytical procedures comparing the gross margin percentage to the prior year to detect unusual fluctuations attributable to cutoff errors

Tracing the last pre-year-end shipping documents to the accounts receivable subsidiary ledger to confirm the sales were recorded before December 31, and tracing the first post-year-end documents to confirm they were recorded in January — verifying that items shipped before year-end are not still in inventory and that items shipped after year-end are not recorded as December sales

explanations.a: Confirming inventory quantities with suppliers verifies the existence and completeness of inventory received, not the accuracy of the shipment cutoff. Cutoff relates to whether shipments were recorded in the correct period — a timing issue, not a quantity issue.
explanations.b: Reviewing count sheets addresses completeness and accuracy of the physical inventory count — it does not directly test whether shipments near year-end were recorded in the correct period. Cutoff testing requires tracing specific shipments to their recording date.
explanations.c: Gross margin analytical procedures may detect cutoff errors if they are large enough to affect the margin — but the analytical procedure provides only general evidence. Direct tracing of specific shipping documents to recorded dates provides more precise and definitive evidence about cutoff accuracy.
explanations.d: This is the classic inventory and accounts receivable cutoff testing procedure. By recording the last document numbers before year-end and the first numbers after year-end, the auditor creates a clear cutoff reference. Then: (1) For pre-year-end shipments — trace those shipping documents to revenue recognition (sales recorded before December 31) and verify those items are not still in the inventory count; (2) For post-year-end shipments — trace to revenue recognition (sales recorded in January) and verify those items were included in the December 31 inventory count. This two-directional testing catches both directions of potential cutoff error.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.keyword: inventory and inventory held by others
questions.text: A manufacturing entity stores a material portion of its finished goods inventory (30% of total inventory) at a public warehouse under a negotiable warehouse receipt arrangement. The inventory was not observed by the auditor during the year-end count because management had not disclosed the off-site location until after the count. How should the auditor address this situation?

answers.text: Accept the warehouse operator's monthly statements as sufficient evidence of the inventory's existence since public warehouses are regulated entities

Perform alternative procedures — including confirming the inventory quantities and condition directly with the warehouse operator, reviewing the negotiable warehouse receipts, and, if the amount is material enough, visiting the warehouse for physical inspection
Exclude the off-site inventory from the audit scope since the auditor was unable to observe it — reducing the scope of the opinion accordingly
Require management to move all inventory to the primary location before the next year-end so the auditor can observe it

explanations.a: Monthly statements from the warehouse operator are management-provided documents — they do not constitute the independent external evidence needed for a 30% inventory balance. Being a regulated entity does not mean the warehouse's records are reliable without independent confirmation. The auditor needs direct corroboration through confirmation or physical inspection.
explanations.b: AU-C Section 501 specifies that when inventory is held by a third party, the auditor should obtain confirmation from the third party about the quantities and condition of the inventory held on behalf of the entity. For material amounts, the auditor should also consider visiting the warehouse to directly observe the inventory. Additionally, the auditor should review the negotiable warehouse receipts — which evidence the entity's legal claim to the inventory — to verify their validity and whether they have been pledged as collateral. These combined procedures provide sufficient evidence about existence and condition for the off-site inventory.
explanations.c: Excluding a material portion (30%) of inventory from the audit scope and issuing a scope-limited opinion is the last resort — not the first response. The auditor should first attempt to obtain sufficient evidence through alternative procedures. Excluding scope is only appropriate if evidence cannot be obtained through any alternative means.
explanations.d: Requiring management to physically relocate inventory before the next year-end is outside the auditor's authority — the auditor cannot dictate business operations. The auditor's role is to obtain sufficient evidence about the inventory as it exists, using the available procedures.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.keyword: inventory and inventory held by others
questions.text: During inventory observation, an auditor notes a large quantity of product that has been sitting in the same location without movement for six months. Tags on the items indicate they are the same model as a product the entity recently discontinued due to poor sales. The auditor's MOST appropriate response is to

answers.text: Complete the inventory observation without noting this item since the auditor's role is to verify quantities, not product saleability

Inquire of management about the specific items, investigate the discontinued product's sales history, evaluate whether the carrying cost exceeds the net realizable value, and assess whether a write-down is needed
Immediately remove the items from the inventory count since they appear obsolete and should not be included in the balance
Accept management's representation that all inventory is saleable since management has responsibility for financial statement presentation

explanations.a: The auditor's inventory observation responsibilities extend beyond merely counting — AU-C 501 requires the auditor to be alert to conditions that may indicate damaged, slow-moving, or obsolete inventory that may require a write-down. Observing conditions that suggest obsolescence and ignoring them would fail the auditor's evidence-gathering obligation.
explanations.b: When the auditor observes indicators of potential obsolescence — specifically, stationary inventory of a recently discontinued product — the appropriate response is investigation and evaluation. The auditor should: (1) inquire of management about the specific items and their plans for disposition; (2) review sales history for this product to assess how it was selling before discontinuation; (3) evaluate whether the current carrying value exceeds the net realizable value (estimated selling price less costs to complete and sell) as required by ASC 330; and (4) assess whether a write-down to NRV is required and whether any such write-down has been recorded.
explanations.c: The auditor cannot remove items from the inventory count — that is management's role. The count is management's count, not the auditor's. The auditor observes and evaluates — not directs inventory management decisions. If items should be written down, that is an accounting judgment, not a physical removal from the count.
explanations.d: Management's representations about inventory saleability supplement but do not substitute for the auditor's own evaluation. When the auditor has observed objective evidence of potential obsolescence (discontinued product, six months of no movement), they cannot simply defer to management's representation — they must independently evaluate whether the carrying value is appropriate.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: The primary purpose of the legal representation letter (attorney letter) in an audit is to

answers.text: Authorize the auditor to obtain privileged attorney-client communications without management's knowledge
Obtain a legal opinion from management's counsel on whether the financial statements are prepared in accordance with GAAP

Obtain corroboration from management's external legal counsel regarding the status of identified litigation and contingencies — including management's estimate of the likely outcome and financial effect — providing independent support for management's representations about these matters
Establish that the auditor is immune from legal claims by obtaining legal counsel's acknowledgment of the auditor's work

explanations.a: Attorney-client communications remain privileged — the legal representation letter does not authorize the auditor to bypass attorney-client privilege. The letter is prepared by management and authorizes their attorney to respond to the auditor's inquiries within the scope management has defined.
explanations.b: The attorney provides information about legal matters — not an opinion on GAAP compliance. The attorney's expertise is in law, not accounting standards. The auditor, not the attorney, evaluates GAAP compliance.
explanations.c: AU-C Section 501 requires the auditor to obtain direct communication from management's external legal counsel about litigation and contingencies. The attorney letter serves to: (1) corroborate management's identification of litigation and contingencies (are there matters management identified but didn't disclose?); (2) provide the attorney's independent assessment of the status and likely outcome of each identified matter; (3) corroborate management's estimates of financial exposure (does the attorney agree with management's assessment of probable loss?); and (4) identify any matters the attorney is aware of that management did not include. This independent corroboration is more reliable than management's representations alone about matters where management has an interest in minimizing perceived exposure.
explanations.d: Attorney letters do not create any legal immunity for auditors. They are an evidentiary procedure to obtain information — not a legal protection mechanism.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: Management discloses a lawsuit in which the plaintiff is seeking $15 million in damages. Management characterizes the outcome as 'reasonably possible' and has not recorded an accrual, only a note disclosure. The attorney's letter states that the range of possible loss is $3 million to $8 million and that the outcome is 'reasonably possible.' How should the auditor evaluate this contingency?

answers.text: The absence of an accrual is appropriate since management and the attorney both characterize the matter as 'reasonably possible' rather than probable — and the note disclosure is consistent with the accounting guidance
The auditor should require management to accrue the full $15 million plaintiff's demand as a conservative measure

The auditor should evaluate whether management has incorrectly assessed the probability as 'reasonably possible' versus 'probable' — and whether the disclosed range ($3M-$8M) is adequately described in the notes to provide users with meaningful information
The auditor should independently review all lawsuit documents to form their own legal opinion about the likely outcome

explanations.a: Under ASC 450, a contingent liability is accrued when it is both probable (likely to occur) and the amount can be reasonably estimated. When the outcome is reasonably possible (more than remote but less than probable), disclosure is required but accrual is not. Since both management and the independent attorney characterize the outcome as 'reasonably possible,' no accrual is required — but the note disclosure must adequately describe the nature of the contingency and the range of possible loss ($3M-$8M). This accounting treatment is appropriate under ASC 450.
explanations.b: Accruing the full plaintiff's demand ($15M) would be inappropriate — the demand amount does not represent management's or the attorney's best estimate of the likely loss. Accruals (when required) are at the best estimate within the range, not the maximum demanded amount.
explanations.c: The auditor should evaluate the adequacy of the accounting treatment and disclosure, but this option suggests the auditor should question whether the characterization is correct — and this questioning is appropriate. However, given that both management and the attorney independently characterized the matter as 'reasonably possible,' the auditor has independent corroboration that 'reasonably possible' (not 'probable') is the appropriate characterization. The primary audit focus should be on the adequacy and completeness of the footnote disclosure, not on challenging the agreed-upon probability assessment.
explanations.d: The auditor is not a legal expert and should not form independent legal opinions about lawsuit outcomes. The auditor relies on management's legal counsel (through the attorney letter) for legal assessments — the auditor evaluates the accounting and disclosure, not the legal merits.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: The auditor requests a legal representation letter regarding a specific regulatory investigation that management disclosed as material. Management's attorney responds that, pursuant to the client's instruction, they cannot provide information about this specific matter because it is covered by attorney-client privilege, and management has not authorized disclosure. How should the auditor evaluate this response?

answers.text: Accept the response since attorney-client privilege is a fundamental legal right — the auditor cannot override it and must accept whatever information the attorney chooses to provide

Treat the attorney's refusal as a scope limitation — since the auditor cannot obtain corroboration for a material disclosed matter, the auditor must evaluate whether alternative procedures can provide sufficient evidence, and if not, consider the effect on the audit opinion
Subpoena the attorney's files to obtain the needed information directly from legal records
Accept management's representation about the matter as sufficient since management has the right to limit the attorney's response

explanations.a: While attorney-client privilege is a legitimate legal right, the failure to obtain corroboration from legal counsel about a material contingency creates an evidence gap — the auditor cannot simply accept the privilege assertion and move on as if sufficient evidence exists. The consequence for the audit is a potential scope limitation, not acceptance of the evidence gap.
explanations.b: When the attorney declines to respond to a specific material matter, the auditor faces a scope limitation on the ability to obtain corroborating evidence from the most relevant independent source. The auditor should: (1) consider whether alternative procedures can provide evidence about the contingency — such as reviewing correspondence between the entity and the regulator, reviewing court filings (which may be public), or obtaining publicly available information about the investigation; (2) if alternative procedures provide sufficient evidence, the limitation is resolved; (3) if the limitation cannot be resolved and the matter is material, the auditor considers the effect on the opinion — potentially a qualified opinion for the scope limitation.
explanations.c: The auditor has no legal authority to subpoena documents. Subpoenas are issued by courts or government agencies — not auditors. Attempting to obtain privileged documents through unauthorized means would be inappropriate and potentially illegal.
explanations.d: Management's representations about legal matters are the least reliable evidence for contingencies — which is why attorney letters exist. If management prevents the attorney from responding about a material matter and management's own representations are the only available evidence, the auditor has a scope limitation that typically requires at minimum a qualified opinion.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: Management has accrued $500,000 for a patent infringement lawsuit. The attorney's letter states that the range of likely loss is $800,000 to $1,200,000 and that the outcome is probable. Management explains the lower accrual by noting that they expect to win a counterclaim that would reduce the net exposure. The attorney did not mention the counterclaim. How should the auditor evaluate this situation?

answers.text: Accept management's accrual since they have relevant information about the counterclaim that the attorney may not have addressed in the letter

Investigate management's claim about the counterclaim by requesting an updated attorney response that specifically addresses the counterclaim and its effect on the probable loss estimate — and if the likely net exposure remains above $500,000, evaluate whether an adjustment is required
Adjust the accrual upward to the maximum of the range ($1,200,000) to be conservative
Accept the $500,000 accrual as within the range of acceptable estimates since the actual liability will be determined in court

explanations.a: Management's explanation about the counterclaim is a new piece of information that requires independent corroboration — not simply acceptance. If the counterclaim significantly affects the likely net exposure, this should have been disclosed to and assessed by management's attorney. The absence of any mention of the counterclaim in the attorney's letter raises questions about whether the attorney is aware of it and whether it genuinely affects the likely outcome.
explanations.b: The attorney's letter indicates a probable loss range of $800,000-$1,200,000 — significantly higher than management's $500,000 accrual. Management introduces a counterclaim as the explanation for the lower accrual, but the attorney who assessed the case did not address it. The auditor should: (1) request that management authorize the attorney to specifically address the counterclaim and its effect on the probable loss estimate; (2) evaluate the updated response to determine the net probable loss incorporating both the lawsuit and the counterclaim; (3) if the net probable loss remains above $500,000 (and the amount can be reasonably estimated), evaluate whether management should increase the accrual; and (4) if management declines to adjust, assess the materiality of the understatement and consider the effect on the opinion.
explanations.c: ASC 450 requires accrual at the best estimate within the range — if no single amount is a better estimate, the minimum of the range is used. Accruing at the maximum ($1,200,000) would be overly conservative and not in accordance with ASC 450.
explanations.d: The fact that the final liability will be determined in court does not allow management to accrue an amount below the probable range without justification. ASC 450 requires the best estimate of probable loss — the range provided by the attorney ($800K-$1.2M) is the most reliable evidence of that estimate, and the $500K accrual falls well below that range without independent support for the counterclaim offset.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: Under AU-C Section 570, the auditor's responsibility regarding going concern is to

answers.text: Predict with certainty whether the entity will survive for the next five years based on current financial trends
Guarantee the entity's financial viability for the period covered by the audit report
Certify that management's going concern assessment is mathematically precise and free of error

Evaluate whether substantial doubt exists about the entity's ability to continue as a going concern for a reasonable period — defined as within 12 months after the financial statements are available to be issued

explanations.a: The auditor does not predict the entity's long-term financial survival with certainty — such a guarantee would be beyond the limits of any professional engagement. The auditor evaluates substantial doubt for a specific near-term period (12 months), not a long-term forecast.
explanations.b: The auditor cannot guarantee financial viability — management and governance are responsible for the entity's going concern. The auditor's role is to evaluate and report on whether substantial doubt exists based on available information, not to ensure survival.
explanations.c: Going concern assessment involves significant judgment and uncertainty — precision and freedom from error are not achievable in this context. The auditor evaluates whether management's assessment is reasonable, not whether it is mathematically precise.
explanations.d: AU-C Section 570 establishes the auditor's responsibility: evaluate whether there is substantial doubt about the entity's ability to continue as a going concern for a reasonable period of time. The reasonable period is defined as within 12 months after the date the financial statements are available to be issued. Within this timeframe, the auditor assesses conditions and events that may raise substantial doubt and evaluates management's plans to address those conditions.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: Which of the following conditions would MOST likely prompt the auditor to consider whether substantial doubt about going concern exists?

answers.text: The entity experienced a 5% decline in gross profit margin due to increased raw material costs, consistent with industry trends
The entity has recurring operating losses for three consecutive years, negative working capital, and has received a default notice from its primary lender due to covenant violations
The entity changed its fiscal year-end from December 31 to September 30, creating a short transitional reporting period
The entity's external auditor from two years ago issued a qualified opinion for a change in accounting principle

explanations.a: A modest decline in gross margin consistent with industry-wide cost trends is a performance concern, but it does not rise to the level of going concern indicators absent other significant issues. AU-C 570 defines specific indicators — recurring operating losses, working capital deficiencies, and inability to service debt — that are more directly relevant.
explanations.b: AU-C Section 570 identifies several conditions that individually or collectively may raise substantial doubt: (1) Recurring operating losses — sustained losses depleting equity and eroding the entity's financial base; (2) Negative working capital — inability to meet short-term obligations with current assets; and (3) Debt covenant violations and lender default notices — immediate threat of debt acceleration, which could force insolvency. The combination of all three of these conditions creates a serious and immediate going concern risk that the auditor must evaluate.
explanations.c: A change in fiscal year creates a short reporting period — an administrative and accounting transition. It does not indicate financial distress or inability to continue operations and is not a going concern indicator.
explanations.d: A prior qualified opinion for an accounting principle change is not a going concern indicator. Prior-year modified opinions for accounting matters do not indicate financial distress — they reflect accounting presentation differences, not operational viability concerns.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: After identifying conditions that raise substantial doubt about going concern, the auditor evaluates management's plans to mitigate the doubt. Which factor is MOST important in that evaluation?

answers.text: Whether management's plans are feasible, whether management has the ability to implement them, and whether they are likely to be effective enough to alleviate substantial doubt for the 12-month period — assessed based on objective evidence, not just management's assertion
Whether the entity's auditors in the prior year raised going concern issues, which would validate the current-year concern
Whether management's plans were developed before or after the auditor identified the going concern indicators
Whether management's plans are documented in board minutes and approved by those charged with governance

explanations.a: AU-C Section 570 requires the auditor to evaluate management's plans by assessing whether they are: (1) feasible — can they realistically be accomplished given the entity's current situation? (e.g., is the proposed asset sale realistic given current market conditions?); (2) within management's ability to implement — does management have the organizational capacity, legal authority, and counterparties needed to execute the plan?; and (3) likely to be effective enough to alleviate substantial doubt — will the plans, if successful, provide sufficient liquidity and financial resources to sustain operations for the 12-month period? This evaluation is based on objective evidence (signed letters of intent, committed financing, actual cost reduction achievements) rather than management's optimistic assertions alone.
explanations.b: Whether prior-year auditors raised going concern concerns is historical context — it does not determine whether current-year plans are effective. Going concern is evaluated based on current conditions and current-period plans, not historical patterns of auditor opinions.
explanations.c: The timing of when management developed the plans is not the primary evaluative criterion. Whether plans were developed before or after the auditor identified concerns may inform the auditor's skepticism, but the substance of the plans (feasibility and effectiveness) is what matters most.
explanations.d: Board approval and documentation are governance factors that provide context about commitment to the plans — but they do not determine whether the plans are actually feasible or effective. A plan can be documented and board-approved and still be unrealistic or insufficient to address the going concern.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: After evaluating management's plans, the auditor concludes that substantial doubt about the entity's going concern still exists, but the financial statements have been properly prepared — including adequate disclosure of the going concern uncertainty. Under AU-C Section 570, what form of audit opinion and reporting is appropriate?

answers.text: An unmodified opinion with a going concern emphasis-of-matter paragraph that describes the conditions and events giving rise to the substantial doubt and refers to the relevant note disclosure
An adverse opinion — if the entity cannot demonstrate it will survive, the financial statements are considered misstated
A qualified opinion for a scope limitation, since the auditor cannot determine the entity's future viability
A disclaimer of opinion, since the going concern uncertainty prevents the auditor from forming any conclusion about the financial statements

explanations.a: Under AU-C Section 570, when substantial doubt about going concern remains after evaluating management's plans, but the financial statements have been properly prepared under the applicable financial reporting framework — including adequate note disclosure of the going concern uncertainty — the auditor issues an unmodified (clean) opinion on the financial statements, accompanied by a separate emphasis-of-matter paragraph that: (1) describes the conditions and events giving rise to substantial doubt; (2) states that substantial doubt exists; and (3) refers users to the relevant note disclosures. The unmodified opinion is appropriate because the financial statements are fairly presented — the going concern matter is disclosed, not hidden.
explanations.b: An adverse opinion is issued when the financial statements are materially misstated. If management has properly disclosed the going concern uncertainty, the financial statements are not misstated — they reflect the circumstances accurately. An adverse opinion would only apply if management refused to include adequate going concern disclosures.
explanations.c: The going concern situation is not a scope limitation — the auditor can fully evaluate the financial statements and reach a conclusion. A scope limitation arises when the auditor cannot obtain sufficient evidence for a material assertion — which is distinct from a going concern situation where evidence is available but the conclusion indicates financial distress.
explanations.d: A disclaimer of opinion is issued when the auditor cannot form any opinion due to an inability to obtain sufficient evidence (pervasive scope limitation). The going concern situation does not prevent the auditor from evaluating the financial statements — the auditor has formed a conclusion (they are fairly presented with adequate disclosure). A disclaimer would only apply if the going concern situation itself created such pervasive uncertainty that the financial statements had no reliability.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: An entity has a $40 million term loan maturing in 9 months. Management's going concern assessment concludes no substantial doubt exists because they have signed a non-binding letter of intent (LOI) with a new lender for refinancing. The refinancing has not been finalized, no commitment letter has been issued, the new lender's credit committee has not yet approved the loan, and the LOI contains several conditions precedent to closing. Management has not disclosed any going concern uncertainty in the financial statements. How should the auditor evaluate this situation?

answers.text: Accept management's assessment — an LOI from a credible financial institution demonstrates management's ability to refinance and eliminates substantial doubt

Evaluate whether the LOI provides sufficient certainty to conclude substantial doubt has been alleviated: a non-binding LOI with multiple unmet conditions precedent and no credit committee approval may not constitute sufficiently certain financing; if substantial doubt remains, the auditor should require adequate disclosure and consider the effect on the opinion if management refuses
Issue an unmodified opinion with a going concern paragraph since all debt-maturity situations automatically trigger going concern reporting
Extend the audit period beyond 12 months to determine whether the refinancing actually closes before issuing an opinion

explanations.a: A non-binding LOI with multiple conditions precedent and no credit committee approval is not equivalent to committed financing. AU-C 570 requires the auditor to evaluate whether management's plans provide sufficient mitigation — 'likelihood of mitigation' requires more than a preliminary indication of interest. The critical distinctions are: (1) non-binding — either party can walk away; (2) conditions precedent — the loan will only close if multiple conditions are met (due diligence, financial covenants, collateral requirements); (3) no credit approval — the decision-making body of the lender has not yet agreed to the loan. These factors mean the refinancing is uncertain, and the entity may face a $40M maturity without replacement financing.
explanations.b: The auditor must critically evaluate whether management's plans constitute a sufficient response to the going concern doubt. A non-binding LOI with substantial conditions is significantly weaker evidence of successful refinancing than a committed credit facility or signed loan agreement. The auditor should: assess the likelihood that the refinancing will actually close within the remaining 9 months; consider what happens if the financing falls through (the entity faces a $40M maturity it cannot service); evaluate whether the conditions precedent are routine or substantive; and determine whether, in light of these uncertainties, substantial doubt has actually been alleviated. If substantial doubt remains, the auditor must require adequate going concern disclosure. If management refuses to add disclosure, the auditor considers a qualified or adverse opinion for inadequate disclosure — not just a going concern paragraph.
explanations.c: Not all debt maturities trigger going concern reporting — only those where the entity cannot demonstrate the ability to refinance or repay. If the entity had a committed replacement facility with no conditions, substantial doubt may have been alleviated. The analysis requires evaluation of the specific facts.
explanations.d: The auditor cannot extend the audit period indefinitely to await the outcome of uncertain events. The going concern evaluation is made based on conditions as of the evaluation date — the auditor must reach a conclusion based on available information, not defer the opinion until a future event resolves the uncertainty.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: In a single audit performed under the Uniform Guidance (2 CFR Part 200), what does the auditor test for each major federal program?

answers.text: Compliance with the types of compliance requirements applicable to the program and the effectiveness of internal controls over compliance designed to prevent or detect material noncompliance
The accuracy of management's internal audit reports for each major program
Only the financial statement presentation of federal award expenditures in the Schedule of Expenditures of Federal Awards (SEFA)
Whether all employees working on federal programs have the appropriate professional credentials and background clearances

explanations.a: AU-C Section 935 and the Uniform Guidance require the single audit to include: (1) compliance testing — testing whether the entity complied with the applicable types of compliance requirements (e.g., allowable costs, eligibility, reporting) for each major program; and (2) internal control testing — obtaining an understanding of and testing the design and operating effectiveness of internal controls over compliance (ICoc) relevant to each major program's compliance requirements. Both components are essential to the single audit's compliance assurance.
explanations.b: The auditor independently tests compliance and controls — they do not evaluate whether management's internal audit reports are accurate. The compliance audit is the external auditor's independent assessment, not a review of management's self-monitoring.
explanations.c: Testing only the SEFA presentation would address financial reporting — it would not address whether the entity actually complied with the substantive requirements of the federal programs. The compliance audit requires testing against the applicable compliance requirements, not just financial presentation.
explanations.d: Employee credentials and background clearances are program eligibility requirements for specific programs — they may be tested as compliance requirements if the applicable Compliance Supplement identifies them as such, but this is not a universal testing requirement for all major programs.
