questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: The 2 CFR 200 Compliance Supplement identifies 12 types of compliance requirements. When planning compliance testing for a specific major program, the auditor should

answers.text: Test all 12 compliance requirement types for every major program — regardless of which apply — to ensure complete coverage

Consult the Compliance Supplement to identify which of the 12 types apply to the specific program, focus on those most likely to have material noncompliance, and design procedures responsive to the identified risk for each applicable requirement
Test only the financial reporting and equipment acquisition compliance requirement types, since these are the most commonly misstated
Defer to the federal agency's own compliance assessment rather than performing independent testing

explanations.a: Not all 12 compliance requirement types apply to every federal program. The Compliance Supplement specifies which types apply to each program — testing all 12 types for a program where only 4 or 5 apply would be inefficient and inconsistent with the risk-based single audit approach.
explanations.b: The risk-based approach to single audit compliance testing requires: (1) identifying which compliance requirement types apply to the specific major program using the Compliance Supplement; (2) assessing the risk of material noncompliance for each applicable requirement — considering factors such as program complexity, prior findings, and control effectiveness; and (3) designing compliance testing procedures specifically responsive to the applicable requirements and the assessed risk level. The Compliance Supplement also identifies suggested audit procedures for each requirement type within each program.
explanations.c: Financial reporting and equipment acquisition are among the 12 types — but they are not universally the most significant. The applicable types and their relative importance vary by program. For example, eligibility requirements may be far more significant for a social services grant than equipment requirements.
explanations.d: The single audit is performed by an independent auditor — not deferred to the federal agency's own assessment. Independent compliance testing by an auditor is the fundamental mechanism of the single audit framework.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: Under the Uniform Guidance, a 'questioned cost' arises when the auditor identifies

answers.text: A cost that management has voluntarily returned to the federal agency as a refund
A cost that exceeded the budgeted amount in the entity's approved program budget by more than 10%
A transaction that was audited in a prior year and found to be compliant — making it unnecessary to retest in the current year

A cost that the auditor believes may not be allowable under the applicable federal program requirements — either because it lacks adequate supporting documentation, was not authorized under applicable regulations, or appears unallowable based on the program's statutory requirements

explanations.a: Voluntary refunds to the federal agency represent management's corrective action — they do not define a questioned cost. A questioned cost is identified by the auditor during testing, not by management's voluntary return of funds.
explanations.b: Exceeding a budgeted amount by more than 10% is not the definition of a questioned cost. While budget compliance may be a monitored metric, a questioned cost relates to allowability under federal requirements — not to internal budget variance thresholds.
explanations.c: A transaction audited and found compliant in a prior year is a prior-period tested item — it does not generate a questioned cost. Questioned costs arise from the auditor's assessment that a cost may be unallowable in the current period.
explanations.d: 2 CFR § 200.1 defines a questioned cost as a cost that is questioned by the auditor because of (1) an audit finding that resulted from a violation or possible violation of a statute, regulation, or the terms and conditions of the federal award; (2) a cost at the time of the audit that is not supported by adequate documentation; or (3) a cost that appears unreasonable and does not reflect the actions a prudent person would take. Questioned costs are reported in the Schedule of Findings and Questioned Costs included in the single audit report package.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: After performing compliance testing, the auditor identifies a material weakness in internal control over compliance (ICoc) for a major federal program. Where and how must this finding be reported?

answers.text: Only in the management letter — material weaknesses in ICoc are communicated informally and are not included in the public single audit report

The finding must be reported in the Schedule of Findings and Questioned Costs and in the report on internal control over compliance — both of which are components of the single audit report package that is submitted to the Federal Audit Clearinghouse
The finding must be reported directly to the Office of Inspector General of the relevant federal agency within 24 hours of discovery
Material weaknesses in ICoc are not separately reportable — they are subsumed within the compliance opinion on major programs

explanations.a: Material weaknesses in ICoc are formal reportable findings — they must appear in the public single audit report package, not just in an informal management letter. The single audit's transparency requirements mandate public reporting of significant compliance control failures.
explanations.b: Under the Uniform Guidance (2 CFR § 200.516), the auditor must report the following in the Schedule of Findings and Questioned Costs: (1) significant deficiencies and material weaknesses in ICFR; (2) significant deficiencies and material weaknesses in ICoc over major programs; (3) material noncompliance with compliance requirements for major programs; and (4) known or likely questioned costs exceeding $25,000. The report on internal control over compliance (a separate required report in the single audit package) must also describe any identified material weaknesses or significant deficiencies in ICoc. The entire report package is submitted to the Federal Audit Clearinghouse and made publicly available.
explanations.c: There is no requirement for the auditor to directly report findings to the federal agency's OIG within any specific timeframe. The reporting mechanism is submission of the single audit report package to the Federal Audit Clearinghouse, where federal agencies can access findings. Direct reporting to OIGs may occur in specific circumstances related to suspected fraud, but is not the standard reporting requirement for ICoc material weaknesses.
explanations.d: Material weaknesses in ICoc are separately reportable findings — they are not merged into the compliance opinion. The compliance audit results in two separate opinions/reports: one on compliance with requirements for major programs, and one specifically on internal control over compliance.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: During compliance testing for a federal education grant, the auditor identifies $180,000 of costs charged to the grant that appear to be general administrative expenses that should not be allocated to this restricted program. Total expenditures under this grant are $3.2 million. Management characterizes the cost allocation as a reasonable administrative judgment. How should the auditor evaluate and respond to this finding?

answers.text: Accept management's characterization since cost allocation decisions involve professional judgment and management has the right to make reasonable allocation decisions
Treat the $180,000 as immaterial since it represents less than 6% of total program expenditures, which is below the 10% threshold for reportable noncompliance

Evaluate whether the costs meet the allowability criteria for the program; if they are not allowable, report the $180,000 as a questioned cost and material noncompliance finding, regardless of management's characterization — and assess whether the allocation represents a systemic issue affecting other periods or programs
Report the matter only if the amounts have been demanded for return by the federal awarding agency, since questioned costs are not reportable until the agency makes a determination

explanations.a: Management's characterization of a cost allocation as 'reasonable' does not override the objective compliance requirements. Federal cost principles (2 CFR Part 200, Subpart E) define allowable costs with specificity — general administrative expenses may only be charged to federal programs under specific conditions (approved indirect cost rates, direct allocation methods). The auditor must independently evaluate whether the costs meet the applicable standards, not simply defer to management's judgment.
explanations.b: The Uniform Guidance does not establish a universal percentage threshold for materiality in single audits. The concept of material noncompliance is assessed based on the nature of the requirement, the amount, and the potential effect on program objectives. More importantly, questioned costs exceeding $25,000 must be reported in the Schedule of Findings regardless of a percentage threshold. $180,000 far exceeds the $25,000 threshold.
explanations.c: The auditor must evaluate whether the $180,000 of costs meet the allowability criteria under the specific grant's requirements and applicable federal cost principles (2 CFR Part 200). If the costs are not allowable: (1) the $180,000 must be reported as a questioned cost in the Schedule of Findings and Questioned Costs; (2) the auditor must assess whether the improper allocation constitutes material noncompliance with the allowable costs requirement; (3) the auditor should evaluate whether similar costs were charged in prior periods (systemic issue) or to other federal programs (cross-program contamination); and (4) the compliance opinion for the program must reflect any identified material noncompliance.
explanations.d: Questioned costs are identified and reported by the auditor based on the audit findings — they are not contingent on the federal agency first demanding repayment. The auditor's reporting obligation exists at the time of the audit finding, not after the agency takes action.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: AU-C Section 450 identifies three types of misstatements the auditor accumulates during an audit. Which of the following correctly describes these three types?

answers.text: Factual misstatements (no doubt the amount is wrong), judgmental misstatements (differences from management estimates the auditor considers unreasonable), and projected misstatements (best estimate of population misstatement extrapolated from sampling)
Material misstatements, immaterial misstatements, and borderline misstatements
Revenue misstatements, expense misstatements, and balance sheet misstatements — classified by the financial statement element affected
Intentional misstatements (fraud), unintentional misstatements (error), and disclosure misstatements (omissions)

explanations.a: AU-C Section 450 specifies three types of misstatements: (1) Factual misstatements — amounts about which there is no doubt, such as a mathematical error, an incorrect application of accounting policy, or a transaction recorded at the wrong amount; (2) Judgmental misstatements — differences between management's accounting estimates and the auditor's best estimate of the amount — when the auditor believes management's estimate is outside a reasonable range or reflects management bias; and (3) Projected misstatements — the auditor's best estimate of misstatements in a population based on results of sampling. For example, if a sample reveals errors totaling $50,000 in a $500,000 sample from a $5 million population, the projected misstatement is $500,000.
explanations.b: Classifying misstatements by materiality level (material vs. immaterial) is a characteristic used to evaluate misstatements, not a typology. AU-C 450 classifies misstatements by their nature and how they arise, not by their quantitative size.
explanations.c: Classifying misstatements by financial statement element (revenue, expense, balance sheet) is an organizational approach to tracking, not the AU-C 450 typology. A single factual or judgmental misstatement may affect multiple financial statement elements.
explanations.d: The distinction between intentional and unintentional misstatements is important for fraud risk assessment (AU-C 240) — but it is not the AU-C 450 typology for accumulating and evaluating misstatements during the audit.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: During an audit, the auditor identifies the following misstatements: (1) a $95,000 factual overstatement of accounts receivable (a billing error); (2) a $130,000 judgmental understatement of the warranty reserve (the auditor's estimate exceeds management's by $130,000); and (3) a $60,000 projected misstatement in inventory from sampling. The auditor has set overall materiality at $250,000 and performance materiality at $180,000. What action should the auditor take regarding these misstatements?

answers.text: No action is needed since each individual misstatement is below overall materiality
Communicate only the $130,000 judgmental misstatement since it is the only one involving accounting judgment
Accept all three misstatements without communication since together they total $285,000 — which is close to but not definitively proven to exceed overall materiality

Communicate all identified misstatements to management and request correction; evaluate whether the aggregate ($285,000) — which exceeds performance materiality ($180,000) and approaches overall materiality ($250,000) — requires additional procedures or opinion consideration if management declines to correct

explanations.a: Evaluating misstatements only individually ignores the aggregate evaluation required by AU-C 450. Even when each misstatement is individually below overall materiality, the aggregate must be evaluated — and an aggregate of $285,000 that exceeds performance materiality ($180,000) and approaches overall materiality ($250,000) requires action.
explanations.b: AU-C 450 requires the auditor to communicate all identified misstatements — factual, judgmental, and projected — to management, not just those involving judgment. Management needs complete information to make informed decisions about corrections.
explanations.c: Accepting misstatements without communication because their aggregate effect is uncertain is not appropriate. AU-C 450 requires the auditor to communicate misstatements to management and evaluate their aggregate effect. Uncertainty about whether the aggregate is material does not eliminate the communication obligation.
explanations.d: AU-C Section 450 requires: (1) communicating all identified misstatements to management at an appropriate level; (2) requesting management to correct the misstatements; and (3) evaluating whether uncorrected misstatements, individually or in aggregate, are material. The aggregate of $285,000 exceeds performance materiality ($180,000) — signaling that the combination warrants attention — and approaches overall materiality ($250,000). If management declines to correct, the auditor must evaluate whether the remaining aggregate (with sampling uncertainty) could exceed overall materiality, potentially requiring additional procedures and/or an opinion modification.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: An audit identifies a $40,000 misstatement in advertising expense — the amount, while below overall materiality of $150,000, relates to an invoice from a company owned by the CFO that was not disclosed as a related-party transaction. Management declines to correct the misstatement or add the disclosure. The auditor's MOST appropriate response is to

answers.text: Accept management's decision since the $40,000 amount is below overall materiality and immaterial misstatements need not be corrected

Consider the qualitative significance of the misstatement — the related-party nature may make it material regardless of amount — and evaluate whether the omission of required disclosures constitutes a material misstatement that requires an opinion modification
Issue a disclaimer of opinion since management has refused to correct the matter
Report the matter to the SEC since undisclosed related-party transactions are automatically reportable

explanations.a: A misstatement's materiality cannot be assessed solely by its dollar amount. AU-C 450 and SEC Staff Accounting Bulletin No. 99 establish that qualitative factors can make a numerically small misstatement material. Related-party transactions require disclosure under GAAP — and the omission of a disclosure that would enable users to understand the nature of a transaction involving the CFO's company may be material regardless of the $40,000 amount.
explanations.b: The qualitative characteristics of this misstatement make it potentially material even at $40,000: (1) it involves a related-party transaction (CFO's company), which requires specific disclosure under ASC 850; (2) management's failure to disclose suggests intentional concealment of a conflict of interest — which would be qualitatively significant to users assessing management integrity; and (3) the disclosure omission is not merely a presentation preference — it is a GAAP-required disclosure. The auditor must evaluate whether the omission is material in the context of the financial statements taken as a whole. If material, and management refuses to correct, the auditor should consider issuing a qualified or adverse opinion for the omission of required disclosures.
explanations.c: A disclaimer of opinion is issued for pervasive scope limitations — not for management's refusal to correct a specific identified misstatement. If the matter is material but not pervasive, a qualified opinion is appropriate. A disclaimer would only apply if the scope limitation were so fundamental that the auditor cannot form any opinion at all.
explanations.d: Auditors do not automatically report undisclosed related-party transactions to the SEC. SEC reporting by external auditors is required in specific limited circumstances (particularly when there is illegal act involving the audit client and management/TCWG decline to take remedial action). An undisclosed related-party transaction does not automatically trigger SEC reporting.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: The auditor has completed field work and accumulated uncorrected misstatements totaling $195,000, against overall materiality of $300,000 and performance materiality of $200,000. Management has declined to correct the misstatements. Additionally, because sampling was used throughout the audit, projected but undetected misstatements likely exist. How should the auditor evaluate whether the financial statements might be materially misstated?

answers.text: The auditor must consider both the identified uncorrected misstatements ($195,000) and the potential for additional undetected misstatements due to sampling risk; since $195,000 approaches overall materiality ($300,000), even a modest amount of undetected misstatement could result in the aggregate exceeding materiality — the auditor should consider whether additional procedures are needed or whether an opinion modification is warranted
The auditor should accept that $195,000 is the total misstatement since all other misstatements would have been detected through the audit procedures
Since $195,000 is below overall materiality ($300,000), no further evaluation is needed and the audit can be concluded with an unmodified opinion
The auditor should automatically issue a qualified opinion whenever uncorrected misstatements exceed performance materiality

explanations.a: AU-C Section 450 requires the auditor to evaluate both identified uncorrected misstatements and the possible additional effect of undetected misstatements. Since sampling was used throughout the audit, the projected misstatements from sampling (even if they were not quantified as high) represent real risk that the actual total misstatement exceeds $195,000. Given that the known amount ($195,000) already exceeds performance materiality ($200,000 — wait, $195K is just below $200K performance materiality but very close) and significantly approaches overall materiality ($300,000), the auditor is in a zone where undetected misstatements could readily push the total above overall materiality. The appropriate response is: evaluate the risk carefully, consider whether targeted additional procedures in high-risk areas could reduce this uncertainty, and if the risk of material misstatement cannot be reduced sufficiently, consider the effect on the opinion.
explanations.b: Audit sampling does not detect all misstatements — it provides a statistical basis for drawing conclusions about the population, but undetected misstatements always exist (detection risk is not zero). Assuming $195,000 is the total misstatement would be incorrect.
explanations.c: Comparing identified misstatements only to overall materiality — without considering sampling risk and undetected misstatements — overstates the auditor's confidence. The $195,000 of identified uncorrected misstatements is close to the $300,000 overall materiality threshold; adding any reasonable estimate of undetected sampling error could push the total above materiality.
explanations.d: Exceeding performance materiality triggers additional evaluation and communication — not automatic opinion modification. An unmodified opinion may still be appropriate if management corrects the misstatements, or if the auditor concludes after additional analysis that the aggregate is unlikely to be material. A qualified opinion is only issued when the auditor concludes that a material misstatement exists and management has not corrected it.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: During testing, the auditor identifies a control deficiency in which the entity's IT department can make changes to the payroll master file (adding employees, changing pay rates) without any independent review or approval. In classifying this deficiency, the auditor determines that an unauthorized change could result in a misstatement of payroll expense that could be material. This deficiency MOST LIKELY constitutes

answers.text: A control deficiency that does not rise to the level of a significant deficiency since it is limited to the IT department
An acceptable compensating control since payroll is reviewed by management after each pay cycle
A significant deficiency requiring written communication to management and TCWG but not a material weakness since payroll errors are typically detected through reconciliation

A material weakness — the lack of independent review over master file changes creates a reasonable possibility that a material misstatement in payroll could be introduced and not detected on a timely basis, satisfying the definition of a material weakness

explanations.a: The scope of a control deficiency is not limited to departmental boundaries. The ability to make unreviewed changes to payroll master files — setting pay rates, adding fictitious employees — is a pervasive risk that affects all payroll transactions, regardless of which department executes the changes. The potential magnitude of undetected payroll fraud from this deficiency is what determines its severity.
explanations.b: After-the-fact management review of payroll totals may detect large anomalies — but it is not equivalent to preventive controls over individual master file changes. Management reviewing aggregate payroll amounts would not necessarily detect a subtle, ongoing unauthorized pay rate increase or a ghost employee added to the master file, particularly if the amounts were calibrated to avoid detection.
explanations.c: If the deficiency creates a reasonable possibility of a material misstatement that would not be detected on a timely basis, it is a material weakness — not merely a significant deficiency. The availability of after-the-fact reconciliations does not automatically reduce the classification to significant deficiency if those reconciliations would not detect the specific type of error the deficiency enables.
explanations.d: A material weakness is a deficiency (or combination of deficiencies) in internal control such that there is a reasonable possibility that a material misstatement of the financial statements will not be prevented, or detected and corrected, on a timely basis (AU-C 265). The absence of independent review over payroll master file changes means that unauthorized changes (fictitious employees, inflated pay rates) could be introduced and persist undetected through normal payroll processing. Given that payroll is typically a material expense, an undetected unauthorized master file change could produce a material payroll misstatement — satisfying the material weakness definition.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: An auditor identifies three control deficiencies: (1) cash disbursements authorization controls fail for transactions between $5,000 and $25,000, with 7 of 50 tested items lacking proper approval — an individually significant deficiency; (2) petty cash reconciliation is performed only annually rather than monthly — an individually minor deficiency; (3) the quarterly review of vendor master file changes by the controller is performed but is not documented — also an individually minor deficiency. Evaluating these deficiencies in combination, which conclusion is MOST appropriate?

answers.text: Each deficiency must be classified independently — the standards do not permit combining deficiencies that affect different areas
Since deficiencies 2 and 3 are individually minor, only deficiency 1 (the significant deficiency) requires written communication

The auditor should evaluate whether the three deficiencies together — when their combined effect on the risk of material misstatement is considered — create a reasonable possibility of a material undetected misstatement, which would elevate the combination to a material weakness requiring written communication to both management and TCWG
The auditor should wait until misstatements are actually detected in the accounts affected by these deficiencies before elevating the combined classification to a material weakness

explanations.a: AU-C 265 explicitly acknowledges that combinations of deficiencies may have a more severe effect than any individual deficiency. The auditor must evaluate whether individually less-severe deficiencies, when considered together, constitute a significant deficiency or material weakness — the standards require this combined evaluation.
explanations.b: Minor deficiencies individually may not require written TCWG communication — but when they combine with a significant deficiency to create an elevated overall risk, the combined classification must be evaluated. Additionally, minor deficiencies that are pervasive across multiple control areas (cash, master file changes) may indicate a broader tone or culture issue.
explanations.c: AU-C Section 265 requires the auditor to evaluate each identified deficiency individually AND to evaluate whether multiple deficiencies that affect the same or related processes should be considered together. In this case: (1) failed authorization for mid-range disbursements (significant deficiency) + (2) infrequent petty cash reconciliation (minor but creates a window for misappropriation) + (3) undocumented vendor master file review (minor but reduces the review's effectiveness as a preventive control) — collectively these create a control environment around cash disbursements where multiple layers of protection are weakened simultaneously. The auditor should assess whether this combination creates a reasonable possibility of a material undetected misstatement in the cash disbursements cycle — and if so, classify and communicate the combination as a material weakness.
explanations.d: Waiting for actual misstatements to classify deficiencies contradicts the preventive purpose of internal control communication. Material weakness classification is based on the potential for misstatement — not on actual detected misstatements. By the time misstatements are detected, the control failure has already occurred.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: Under AU-C Section 580, when should the written representations letter from management be dated?

answers.text: The date field work commenced — to document that management's representations were in place throughout the audit
As of the date of the auditor's report — management's representations are contemporaneous with the opinion being issued
The last day of the fiscal year being audited — to ensure representations relate specifically to the balance sheet date
A date chosen by management's legal counsel to align with their indemnification terms

explanations.a: The date field work commenced is not the appropriate date for the representations letter. Written representations cover the entire period of the audit, including events through the completion of field work — not just the period from field work's start.
explanations.b: AU-C Section 580.22 specifies that the date of the written representations shall be as of the date of the auditor's report. This ensures management's representations cover the period from the balance sheet date through the date of the report — including subsequent events — and are contemporaneous with the auditor's conclusions as expressed in the report. If management cannot or will not provide representations dated as of the report date, the auditor has a significant issue affecting the ability to issue the report.
explanations.c: The fiscal year-end date is the balance sheet date — not the appropriate date for the representations letter. The representations must cover events through the report date, which occurs after the fiscal year-end.
explanations.d: Legal counsel's indemnification terms are commercial and legal arrangements that have no bearing on the required timing of management's representations. The timing is governed by AU-C 580, not by separate legal agreements.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: Which of the following is a required element of the written representations management must provide in a financial statement audit?

answers.text: Management's assertion that the financial statements are fairly presented in all material respects in accordance with the applicable financial reporting framework, along with acknowledgment of responsibility for the financial statements and ICFR
A representation that management has provided the auditor with all unrestricted access to personnel and information, and that all known instances of fraud have been disclosed to the auditor
A representation that the entity will maintain the same accounting policies for the next three fiscal years to facilitate comparative analysis
Management's guarantee that no material misstatements exist in the financial statements for the audited period

explanations.a: AU-C Section 580 specifies several required representations, including: (1) management's acknowledgment of its responsibility for the preparation of the financial statements in accordance with the applicable framework; (2) management's representation that the financial statements are fairly presented (for nonissuers) or that there are no material misstatements (the framing varies); (3) management's acknowledgment of its responsibility for designing and maintaining internal control; and (4) management's belief about the effects of uncorrected misstatements. These representations are fundamental to the audit — they establish the basis on which the auditor can issue an opinion and confirm that management has provided complete and accurate information.
explanations.b: While the representations letter typically includes a representation about access to information and about fraud disclosure, combining these into a single option and labeling it the 'required element' understates the full set of required representations. Option c more precisely captures the core required representations under AU-C 580.
explanations.c: A commitment to maintain accounting policies for future periods is not a required representation — management has the right to change accounting policies in accordance with applicable standards. Written representations address past and present facts, not forward-looking commitments about accounting policy stability.
explanations.d: Written representations are management's assertions — not guarantees. Management represents that the financial statements are fairly presented to the best of their knowledge; they cannot guarantee the complete absence of material misstatements. The distinction between a representation and a guarantee is important — the auditor independently evaluates the financial statements rather than relying on a management guarantee.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: Written representations in an audit engagement must be provided by which level of management?

answers.text: Management with overall responsibility for the entity and its financial reporting — typically the CEO (or equivalent) and CFO (or equivalent), not mid-level managers or department heads
All members of the accounting department who processed transactions during the audit period
The board of directors as a collective body — they bear ultimate responsibility for the financial statements
Any management member chosen by the audit committee, based on their specific knowledge of the matters represented

explanations.a: AU-C Section 580.09 requires written representations from management with overall responsibility for the entity and knowledge of the matters represented. In practice, this typically means the CEO (or president) and CFO (or controller) who bear primary responsibility for the organization's financial reporting. These individuals have the authority and knowledge to make binding representations on behalf of the entity about the financial statements and the information provided to the auditors.
explanations.b: All accounting department members providing representations would be impractical and is not required. Representations are made by senior management with overall responsibility — not by operational staff who processed individual transactions. Representations cover the financial statements as a whole, not individual transaction processing.
explanations.c: The board of directors exercises governance oversight but does not itself prepare the financial statements or have operational management responsibility. Representations are required from management, not from the governance body. The board receives communication from the auditor (under AU-C 260) but does not sign the representations letter.
explanations.d: Representations must come from management with overall responsibility — the selection is not at the audit committee's discretion or based on specific knowledge of individual items. The standard is the level of management with ultimate responsibility for the entity's financial statements.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: An auditor is auditing an entity's pension obligation, which is a complex Level 3 accounting estimate. Management provides a written representation confirming that the pension liability is fairly stated. Why is this representation, standing alone, INSUFFICIENT as audit evidence for the valuation assertion?

answers.text: It is insufficient because AU-C 580 prohibits using representations for pension obligations — a specialist opinion is always required instead
It is insufficient because written representations must be notarized to be valid audit evidence, and unnotarized representations cannot be relied upon

It is insufficient because the representation comes from management — the same party responsible for preparing the estimate — and cannot independently corroborate the reasonableness of complex assumptions they themselves developed; independent evidence (actuarial evaluation, specialist opinion, comparison to independent benchmarks) is required
It is insufficient only if the representation was not co-signed by the entity's external actuary

explanations.a: AU-C 580 does not categorically prohibit using representations for pension obligations. Written representations are required in all audits and are valid evidence — the issue is their sufficiency when standing alone. A specialist opinion may be advisable but is not universally required in all circumstances.
explanations.b: There is no notarization requirement for written representations in auditing. AU-C 580 specifies the form and content of representations but does not require notarization.
explanations.c: AU-C Section 580.04 explicitly states that written representations do not provide sufficient appropriate audit evidence on their own about any of the matters with which they deal. For a complex Level 3 pension estimate, management's representation that the liability is fairly stated is essentially management attesting to the reliability of management's own work — it provides no independent corroboration. The auditor must independently evaluate the actuarial assumptions, test the data used, and assess whether the estimate falls within a reasonable range using evidence from sources other than management's own representations.
explanations.d: Co-signing by the external actuary would make the representations more informative about the actuary's involvement, but the fundamental issue is independence and corroboration from sources other than management. Even actuary co-signing would not make management's representations alone sufficient — independent evaluation of the actuarial methodology and assumptions is still required.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.text: Near the completion of an audit, management refuses to provide a written representation confirming that all known instances of actual or suspected fraud have been disclosed to the auditor. Management's stated reason is that they 'cannot make such a broad statement without consulting with legal counsel.' The auditor's MOST appropriate response is to

answers.text: Issue the audit report without the representation since management's legal consultation concern is reasonable and representations are merely corroborative evidence
Accept a modified representation in which management states only that 'to the best of management's knowledge, there are no known instances of fraud' — omitting the reference to suspected fraud

Evaluate the implications of management's refusal, determine whether the refusal indicates a scope limitation or raises questions about the reliability of other representations obtained, and consider whether to modify the opinion or withdraw from the engagement
Proceed with issuing an unmodified opinion since the audit procedures performed independently established that no fraud exists

explanations.a: Written representations are required by AU-C 580 — they are not optional corroborative evidence that can be omitted based on management's preference. If required representations are not provided, the auditor has a scope limitation and must evaluate the effect on the opinion and the engagement.
explanations.b: A modified representation that omits the reference to suspected fraud removes a critical element. AU-C 580 requires representations about both actual and suspected fraud — the suspected fraud representation is particularly important because it addresses management's awareness of conditions that could indicate fraud, even without certainty. Accepting a diluted version of a required representation is not a solution.
explanations.c: AU-C Section 580.19 specifies that if management does not provide required written representations, the auditor should discuss the matter with management, re-evaluate the integrity of management, and consider the effect on other evidence. If the representations are not provided as required, the auditor may not be able to obtain sufficient appropriate audit evidence. The refusal to represent about fraud may itself indicate management awareness of fraud they do not want to disclose — which would be significant for the auditor's overall assessment. The auditor should consider modifying the opinion for the scope limitation or withdrawing from the engagement if the situation is sufficiently serious.
explanations.d: Audit procedures establish reasonable assurance — not absolute certainty — that no material fraud exists. The absence of detected fraud through audit procedures does not eliminate the need for management's representations. The two types of evidence serve different purposes: procedures detect misstatements; representations document management's knowledge and confirm complete disclosure.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.keyword: subsequent events and subsequently discovered facts
questions.text: In auditing, subsequent events are events or transactions that occur after the balance sheet date but before the audit report is issued. These events are classified into which two types?

answers.text: Favorable events (which must be disclosed) and unfavorable events (which must be accrued)
Quantifiable events (requiring accrual) and non-quantifiable events (not requiring any financial statement recognition)
Material events (requiring both adjustment and disclosure) and immaterial events (requiring neither adjustment nor disclosure)

Recognized events (Type 1 — providing evidence about conditions at the balance sheet date, requiring adjustment) and non-recognized events (Type 2 — new conditions arising after the balance sheet date, requiring disclosure but not adjustment)

explanations.a: The classification is not based on whether events are favorable or unfavorable. A favorable event (e.g., a large new customer contract signed after year-end) and an unfavorable event (e.g., a lawsuit filed after year-end) may both be Type 2 events requiring only disclosure — not accrual.
explanations.b: Quantifiability is relevant to whether a recognized (Type 1) event can be adjusted with a specific dollar amount — but it is not the criterion for classifying subsequent events into their two types. The classification depends on whether the event provides evidence about conditions existing at the balance sheet date.
explanations.c: Materiality affects whether an event needs to be reported in the financial statements — immaterial events generally require neither recognition nor disclosure. However, this is not the two-type classification of subsequent events. The classification is based on whether conditions existed at the balance sheet date.
explanations.d: AU-C Section 560 (and ASC 855 for GAAP purposes) classifies subsequent events into two types: (1) Type 1 (Recognized Subsequent Events) — events that provide additional evidence about conditions that existed at the balance sheet date; these require adjustment of the financial statements to reflect the new information (e.g., a customer that goes bankrupt after year-end but had been deteriorating financially throughout the year — the bad debt existed at year-end); and (2) Type 2 (Non-Recognized Subsequent Events) — events that reflect conditions arising after the balance sheet date; these require disclosure (if material) but not adjustment (e.g., a natural disaster that destroys a plant after year-end — the loss occurred after year-end, not at year-end).

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.keyword: subsequent events and subsequently discovered facts
questions.text: After December 31 (the audit client's year-end), but before the audit report is issued, the auditor learns that a major customer (representing 18% of accounts receivable) filed for bankruptcy on January 15. The customer had been experiencing significant financial difficulties throughout the fourth quarter. This event MOST LIKELY requires

answers.text: No action — events after December 31 are inherently Type 2 subsequent events and cannot require adjustment of December 31 financial statements

Adjustment of the allowance for doubtful accounts at December 31 to reflect the probable uncollectability of this receivable — because the bankruptcy provides evidence of a deteriorating condition that existed at year-end, making this a Type 1 subsequent event
A disclosure-only note describing the January 15 bankruptcy, with no adjustment to the December 31 receivable balance
Immediate withdrawal from the audit engagement since a major customer bankruptcy indicates the client may also face going concern issues

explanations.a: Not all post-balance-sheet events are Type 2. Events are classified based on whether conditions existed at the balance sheet date — not merely based on when the event occurred. A bankruptcy filing in January that arose from deteriorating conditions in the fourth quarter provides evidence of impairment that existed at December 31.
explanations.b: A customer's January bankruptcy — when the customer had been experiencing financial difficulty throughout the fourth quarter — is a Type 1 subsequent event (Recognized). The condition (the customer's inability to pay) existed at December 31, but the definitive evidence of the condition (the bankruptcy filing) came in January. Under ASC 855 and AU-C 560, a Type 1 event provides additional evidence about a condition that existed at the balance sheet date — requiring adjustment of the financial statements rather than only disclosure. The allowance for doubtful accounts at December 31 should be adjusted to reflect the probable uncollectability of the 18% receivable.
explanations.c: Because the condition (deteriorating financial health) existed at December 31, the appropriate treatment is adjustment — not mere disclosure. Disclosure without adjustment would leave the receivable and allowance at their pre-bankruptcy amounts, which would misstate the December 31 balance sheet.
explanations.d: A major customer's bankruptcy is a serious business event requiring careful audit response — but it does not automatically require withdrawal from the engagement. It requires evaluation of the going concern implications for the audit client, adjustment of the allowance, and potential going concern consideration if the client's viability is also threatened.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.keyword: subsequent events and subsequently discovered facts
questions.text: After completing all audit procedures and just before issuing the audit report, the auditor becomes aware that the entity entered into a significant business combination — acquiring a company for $50 million — on February 28 (two months after the December 31 year-end). The acquisition was not disclosed in the financial statements. This is MOST appropriately classified and addressed as

answers.text: A Type 1 subsequent event requiring the acquisition to be recorded in the December 31 financial statements at $50 million
An immaterial event requiring no action since acquisitions completed after year-end do not affect the December 31 balance sheet

A Type 2 subsequent event — the acquisition reflects a new condition arising after December 31, not a condition existing at year-end; management should add a disclosure note describing the acquisition and its financial effects before the audit report is issued
A subsequently discovered fact requiring the auditor to withdraw from the engagement since the acquisition was not communicated before the audit was completed

explanations.a: A $50 million acquisition completed on February 28 is a new condition arising after December 31 — the entity did not own the acquired company at year-end, so there is nothing to record on the December 31 balance sheet. Requiring the acquisition to be recorded in the December 31 financial statements would misrepresent the entity's position at year-end.
explanations.b: A $50 million acquisition is unlikely to be immaterial — and material subsequent events that reflect new conditions must be disclosed even if they do not require balance sheet adjustment. The appropriate classification determines the accounting treatment; dismissing the event without evaluation would not be appropriate.
explanations.c: The acquisition of a company for $50 million on February 28 is a Type 2 subsequent event — it reflects a new condition (the acquisition) that arose after December 31, not evidence of a condition that existed at year-end. Under ASC 855 and AU-C 560, Type 2 events require disclosure (if material) but not adjustment of the financial statements. Management should add a note describing the acquisition (date, entity acquired, consideration paid, preliminary description of the assets and liabilities acquired) before the audit report is issued. The auditor should also evaluate whether the report date needs to be extended to cover this event.
explanations.d: The failure to communicate the acquisition before the audit was completed is a planning and communication deficiency, not a reason to withdraw. The appropriate response is to evaluate the event and require appropriate disclosure before issuing the report.

questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.keyword: subsequent events and subsequently discovered facts
questions.text: An auditor issued an audit report on financial statements dated March 15. On April 8 — after the report was issued but before the annual report was distributed — the auditor discovers that a significant environmental liability existed at December 31 but was concealed by management and is not disclosed in the financial statements. The auditor's MOST appropriate initial response is to

answers.text: Discuss the matter with management and those charged with governance, evaluate whether the financial statements need to be revised to include the omitted disclosure, and if management refuses to revise, consider notifying regulatory authorities and parties relying on the financial statements
Issue a revised audit report dated April 8 with a qualified opinion and distribute it to all parties who received the original report
Take no action since the report has already been issued and the auditor's professional responsibility for that engagement period has concluded
Contact the entity's legal counsel to determine whether the environmental liability requires disclosure and accept their conclusion without independent evaluation

explanations.a: AU-C Section 560.14-.19 addresses subsequently discovered facts — facts that become known after the audit report date. When the auditor discovers that a material fact was not disclosed in the financial statements, the auditor must: (1) discuss the matter with management and TCWG; (2) determine whether the financial statements need to be revised (they do if the omitted fact is material); (3) evaluate management's response — if management refuses to revise the financial statements, the auditor should notify those charged with governance and, if the financial statements have been distributed, consider notifying parties relying on them (such as regulatory authorities or users who received the financial statements) and consider withdrawing from future engagements. The auditor does not simply accept management's concealment of a material liability.
explanations.b: Issuing a new report with a modified opinion is part of the process when financial statements are revised — but the initial response should be discussion with management and TCWG rather than immediately issuing a new report. The sequence is: discuss → request revision → issue revised statements and auditor's report if management agrees.
explanations.c: The auditor's professional responsibility does not end at the date the report is signed. AU-C 560 explicitly creates responsibilities that extend beyond the report date when material facts are discovered afterward, particularly before the financial statements have been distributed to users.
explanations.d: External legal counsel provides legal advice about legal obligations — they do not determine what must be disclosed under GAAP. The auditor must independently evaluate whether the environmental liability meets the disclosure requirements of ASC 450 (contingencies) and related guidance, not defer to legal counsel's conclusions.

questions.certification: Uniform CPA Examination — Auditing and Attestation
questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.keyword: subsequent events and subsequently discovered facts
questions.text: An auditor completes the audit and dates the report March 15. Before the financial statements are issued, a material subsequent event is discovered on March 22 — a lawsuit resulting in a $30 million judgment against the entity. Rather than extending the audit report date (which would require extending all procedures to March 22), the auditor dual-dates the report. What does dual-dating accomplish?

answers.text: Dual-dating allows the auditor to issue two separate audit reports — one for the financial statements and one for the subsequent event — to be distributed to different user groups
Dual-dating allows the auditor to disclaim responsibility for the subsequent event while still issuing an opinion on the financial statements

Dual-dating allows the auditor to include both the original date (March 15) and the specific subsequent event date (March 22) in the report — limiting the extended responsibility to the specific subsequent event rather than requiring re-performance of all procedures through March 22
Dual-dating eliminates the need to disclose the subsequent event in the financial statements since the report date communicates the matter to users

explanations.a: Dual-dating produces a single audit report — not two separate reports. The single report references both dates to communicate the scope of the auditor's responsibility for subsequent events.
explanations.b: Dual-dating does not disclaim responsibility for the subsequent event — it actually acknowledges the event and limits the extension of responsibility specifically to that event. The auditor takes responsibility for the identified subsequent event, not less responsibility.
explanations.c: Dual-dating (as described in AU-C 560) means the auditor includes both the original report date (March 15) and a subsequent date (March 22) specifically for the identified subsequent event. The format 'March 15, 20XX except for Note X, as to which the date is March 22, 20XX' communicates that: (1) the auditor's overall procedures were completed through March 15; and (2) with respect to the specific event in Note X, the auditor has extended responsibility to March 22. This limits the additional work required — instead of extending all procedures to March 22, the auditor only needs to satisfy themselves about the specific subsequent event and its proper disclosure.
explanations.d: Dual-dating does not eliminate the disclosure requirement — it establishes the scope of the auditor's responsibility for the subsequent period. The $30 million judgment must still be disclosed in the financial statements (as a subsequent event in accordance with ASC 855), and the auditor's report communicates the extended date to explain the scope of subsequent event procedures.

questions.name: Performing Further Procedures and Obtaining Evidence
questions.keyword: subsequent events and subsequently discovered facts
questions.text: An audit report was signed March 15. Before the financial statements are issued (scheduled for March 30), the auditor learns of two events: (1) on March 18, a fire destroyed a major manufacturing plant — management estimates $30 million of uninsured damage, and the entity has no business interruption insurance; (2) on March 25, a court announced a $15 million judgment against the entity — this lawsuit was disclosed at December 31 as 'reasonably possible' with no accrual. How should the auditor address these two events?

answers.text: Both events are Type 2 subsequent events requiring disclosure only — the auditor should require management to add notes for both and dual-date the report to March 25
Both events are immaterial relative to the total balance sheet and require no further action before the March 30 issuance

The fire is a new condition (Type 2 event) requiring disclosure and potentially triggering going concern consideration — not adjustment; the court judgment may require reclassification from 'reasonably possible' to 'probable' and an accrual of $15 million (Type 1, if the judgment provides evidence the loss was probable at December 31) — both matters require management to update the financial statements and the auditor to dual-date or extend the report date
The auditor should immediately withdraw from the engagement since the events make the financial statements fundamentally unreliable

explanations.a: Characterizing the court judgment as Type 2 only oversimplifies the analysis. The lawsuit existed at December 31 and was disclosed — the court's decision provides new information about the probability of loss. This may convert the matter from 'reasonably possible' to 'probable,' requiring reclassification and accrual under ASC 450. That would be a Type 1 (recognized) subsequent event for the judgment amount, requiring adjustment rather than merely updated disclosure.
explanations.b: A $30 million uninsured plant fire and a $15 million court judgment are highly material events for virtually any entity. Treating them as immaterial without analysis would be a serious audit failure.
explanations.c: The two events require different treatment: (1) The March 18 plant fire — this is a new condition arising after December 31 (the plant existed and was operational at year-end; it was destroyed afterward). This is a Type 2 subsequent event requiring disclosure rather than balance sheet adjustment. However, the $30 million uninsured loss and loss of production capacity may create or worsen going concern doubt that the auditor must evaluate. (2) The March 25 court judgment — the lawsuit was ongoing at December 31 and already disclosed as 'reasonably possible.' The court's announcement of a judgment is new information about a condition (the litigation) that existed at year-end. This event may constitute evidence that the loss was probable at December 31 — converting the disclosure-only treatment to a requirement for a $15 million accrual (Type 1 event). The auditor must evaluate whether the judgment changes the ASC 450 classification. Both matters require the auditor to dual-date or extend the report date, require updated financial statement disclosures, and potentially require management to record the $15M accrual.
explanations.d: Material subsequent events require careful evaluation and appropriate accounting treatment — they do not automatically require withdrawal. Withdrawal is appropriate when the auditor determines that the financial statements cannot be relied upon (e.g., if management refuses to update disclosures or record the accrual) — but the first step is evaluation and discussion with management, not immediate withdrawal.
